title: Record a speed baseline before changing anything
hypothesis: If we record a dated baseline score, LCP, CLS, INP and TTFB for every key page before touching the site, then we can prove which later fix actually worked because we have a number to compare against.

signal.check: No dated speed baseline or change log exists yet for the store's key templates.

risk.note: Read-only measurement step; nothing on the live site changes.

prerequisites: Access to PageSpeed Insights or a lab testing tool
List of key pages: home, a collection, top product, cart, checkout
steps: Pick home, a collection, the top product page, the ad landing page, cart and checkout as reference pages.
Run PageSpeed Insights on mobile and desktop for each page.
Record score, LCP, CLS, INP, TTFB and the LCP element in a table with the date.
Start a dated change log with this as the first entry.

test.method: Compare the same table after each future change to the store.
test.measure: LCP, CLS, INP, TTFB, PSI score
test.read_point: Immediately, then again 28 days after any fix for field data

title: Find the one biggest cause of slowness before making many small fixes
hypothesis: If we find and fix the single largest cause first, such as a giant hero image or a pile of unused apps, then most of the score gain shows up in one move because that cause explains most of the slowdown.

signal.check: A speed report lists many issues at once and it is not clear which to fix first.

expected_effect.size: largest single opportunity in the report, varies by store

risk.note: This is a reading step, not a change; low risk of breaking anything.

prerequisites: SPD-001 baseline done
steps: Open the PageSpeed Insights report for the top-traffic page.
Hover the score circle to see which metric would most improve the score.
Open that metric's opportunity group first and read the estimated savings.
Fix that item before moving to smaller items in the list.

test.method: Re-run the report after the single biggest fix, before doing anything else.
test.measure: PSI score, and the specific metric flagged as the biggest lever
test.read_point: After 3 averaged runs, 1 to 2 minutes after the change

title: Fix the page paid ads land on before any other page
hypothesis: If we fix the ad landing page first, then paid clicks stop leaving before load, because a slow landing page wastes spend that already bought the click.
does_not_apply_when: Store runs no paid traffic and has no dedicated landing pages

signal.check: Sessions and revenue by template show most paid traffic lands on a product or campaign page with a poor LCP, while home page passes.

risk.note: Order-of-work change, not a risky technical change on its own.

prerequisites: Sessions and revenue by template
List of pages ads land on
steps: Pull sessions and revenue by template (home, collection, product, cart, checkout).
Identify which page paid ads actually land on.
Order the fix list: ad landing pages first, then top product pages, then collections, then home, then cart and checkout.
Run the speed baseline (SPD-001) on the ad landing page specifically.

test.method: Compare landing page LCP and score before and after, and track CPA over the following weeks.
test.read_point: Immediately for LCP, 2 to 4 weeks of spend for CPA

title: Fix content before infrastructure: images and scripts before caching and hosting
hypothesis: If we fix images, scripts and layout stability before touching caching, CDN or hosting, then the infrastructure work actually helps, because caching a heavy page just hides the problem for repeat visitors.

signal.check: A plan proposes caching, a CDN change or a hosting upgrade before images and third-party scripts have been reviewed.

expected_effect.size: unknown, sequencing effect not a standalone number

risk.note: Reordering a plan; no code change by itself.

steps: List all proposed speed fixes for the store.
Group them: images, scripts and apps, layout stability (LCP/CLS), fonts and CSS, then caching, CDN and hosting.
Do the first three groups and re-measure before starting the caching or hosting group.
On Shopify, skip the hosting step entirely; caching and CDN are already managed.

test.method: Confirm images and script fixes are re-measured as done before any caching or hosting ticket opens.
test.read_point: Before starting the caching or hosting group of work

title: Decide how hard to chase the speed score based on paid vs organic traffic share
hypothesis: If a store depends on organic traffic, then pushing the Core Web Vitals score matters more for ranking; if traffic is mostly paid, slow pages still lose clicks even though the score itself matters less for ranking.

signal.check: Paid vs organic session share is known and the store has not decided how far to push speed work.

risk.note: A prioritization decision, not a technical change.

prerequisites: Paid vs organic share of sessions
steps: Pull the paid vs organic share of sessions for the store.
If organic is a meaningful share, treat every flagged Core Web Vitals issue as worth fixing.
If traffic is nearly all paid, still fix slow pages for shopper experience, but do not oversell the SEO angle.
Note visits without sales as a candidate cause to test, not a proven one.

test.method: Track organic clicks and bounce rate on fixed pages over the following weeks.
test.read_point: 4 to 8 weeks after fixes, since organic ranking effects lag

title: Stop chasing a perfect 100 score and drop tools that only game the lab score
hypothesis: If we stop targeting a perfect lab score and instead judge fixes by real shopper experience, then we avoid wasting money on apps that raise the number while shoppers still wait.

signal.check: The store has installed a speed app or plugin whose only visible effect is a higher lab score, with no change in real load feel.

risk.note: Removing a tool that does not help; test before removing to be sure.

steps: List any speed apps, plugins or 'specialists' currently installed.
Run the slow-connection visual test (see the visual test idea) with the tool on and off.
If the real experience does not change, drop the tool.
Set the working target at a mobile score over 50, not 100, for an image-heavy store.

test.method: Compare slow-connection visual test and PSI score with the tool active vs removed.

title: Remove every app, plugin and script that has no clear revenue role
hypothesis: If we write down how each installed app or script makes money today and remove the ones with no answer, then the site gets lighter and faster because third-party script count is the strongest predictor of a poor mobile score.

signal.check: The store has more than 20 installed apps, plugins or hand-pasted scripts, or nobody can say what several of them do.

expected_effect.size: median mobile score 74 at 0-5 third-party services vs 44 at 21-30, in a 1,533-store dataset

risk.note: Removing a script that quietly powers reviews, loyalty or tracking can break a feature; test each one.

prerequisites: List of installed apps, plugins, embeds and scripts with the revenue role of each
steps: List every installed app, sales-channel app, app embed, plugin and hand-pasted script.
For each, write the concrete way it makes money or supports operations right now.
Mark items with no answer, purely visual items, trial leftovers, or duplicates of a theme feature.
Uninstall and delete those marked items completely, not just deactivate.
For anything uncertain, disable on staging, re-measure, then decide.
Re-test the store after each removal so the effect can be attributed.

test.method: Before and after speed test per removed item, plus a full function check.
test.read_point: After each removal, averaged over 3 runs

title: Re-audit speed on a monthly schedule and hold a page weight and script budget
hypothesis: If we test speed monthly, after every app install or theme change, and before big sales, then the store stops sliding backward because most feature additions quietly slow pages.

signal.check: No recurring speed test schedule exists, or the last test was more than a month ago and the store added apps or theme changes since.

expected_effect.size: prevents the score sliding from 60-80 new down to 40 with apps and 20 or lower with heavy customization, per one source's illustration

risk.note: A monitoring habit; no direct site risk.

prerequisites: SPD-001 baseline done
steps: Write a budget: max page weight, minimum mobile score, max third-party scripts per page.
Schedule a speed test at least monthly, and right after any app install, theme change or site-wide update.
Schedule an extra test before major sales.
Review any change that breaks the budget before approving it.

test.method: Track the budget numbers over time in the change log.

title: Build a speed revenue model with the store's own numbers, not a vendor's example
hypothesis: If we model speed's revenue impact from the store's own sessions, conversion rate and AOV, then the founder gets a number they can trust, because a vendor's own case study is not this store's forecast.

signal.check: The store wants a business case for speed work but only has third-party benchmark numbers to point to.

expected_effect.size: direction only; sources cite +5.6% to +8.4% conversion per second or per 0.1s as benchmarks, not a promise

risk.note: A spreadsheet exercise; no code risk.

prerequisites: Daily sessions, conversion rate, AOV, current load time
steps: Multiply daily sessions by conversion rate by AOV to get today's daily revenue.
Choose an assumed conversion lift for a stated speed gain and label it clearly as an assumption.
Recompute daily revenue with the lifted conversion rate and multiply the difference by 365.
Add the wasted ad-spend angle: a paid click that leaves before load never sees the offer.
Do the arithmetic in a spreadsheet or code, not by hand in a slide.

test.method: Compare the modeled lift to the store's own before and after conversion rate once a fix ships.
test.read_point: 28 days after the fix, for a stable comparison

title: Test and optimize speed for mobile first, on a real mid-range device where possible
hypothesis: If we test on mobile with a real or realistic connection instead of a developer machine, then we catch problems that desktop testing hides, because mobile pages load far slower than desktop on average.

signal.check: Mobile share of sessions or revenue is high, or traffic comes mostly from ads, and testing has only been done on a fast desktop connection.

expected_effect.size: mobile pages load about 87.8% longer than desktop on average, per one source

risk.note: A testing practice; no site change on its own.

prerequisites: Mobile share of sessions and revenue
steps: Pull mobile share of sessions and revenue for the store.
Run PageSpeed Insights on the mobile tab first for every template.
Also check the desktop tab, since layout shift can be zero on mobile and large on desktop.
Where possible, load the store on a real mid-range phone on mobile data, not office Wi-Fi.

test.method: Compare mobile and desktop scores and vitals side by side after fixes.

title: Never strip a feature that helps shoppers buy just to win a speed score
hypothesis: If we check a widget's revenue or trust role before removing it for speed, then we avoid losing sales, because reviews, chat and size charts can matter more to conversion than the score.

signal.check: A speed fix list proposes removing reviews, chat, size charts or tracking without checking their sales role first.

expected_effect.size: unknown, protective effect not a lift

risk.note: Removing the wrong widget can cut conversion even as the score improves.

steps: Before removing any widget for speed, write down its revenue or trust role.
Check whether shoppers actually use it, with click maps if available.
If it has a clear role, delay or slim it instead of removing it outright.
Only remove widgets with no answer to 'what does this do for revenue'.

test.method: Track conversion rate on the affected page for at least a week after any removal.

title: Spend speed effort on the levers your platform actually controls
hypothesis: If we match the speed work to the platform, apps and images on Shopify, server and plugins on WordPress, then effort goes where it can actually move the needle instead of on things the platform already handles.

signal.check: A fix list includes hosting or caching work on Shopify, or ignores server and plugin bloat on a self-hosted WordPress or WooCommerce store.

risk.note: A planning decision, not a technical change on its own.

prerequisites: Platform and plan, theme name, who built it
steps: Confirm the platform: Shopify, WordPress/WooCommerce, Shopware or a custom framework.
On Shopify, put effort into apps and images; skip caching scripts and hosting work.
On WordPress or WooCommerce, put effort into hosting, database health and plugin conflicts.
On other platforms, check what the platform already does natively before adding tools.

test.method: Confirm no effort was spent on a lever the platform already handles.

title: Move to a simpler theme instead of endlessly patching an old, feature-heavy one
hypothesis: If we rebuild an old, heavily customized theme on a simple base theme at the next redesign, then speed improves more than patching, because optimizing an old theme can cost more than a rebuild.
does_not_apply_when: Store just launched a modern, lightly customized theme

signal.check: The theme is old, custom-built, or heavily agency-customized, and a redesign is already planned or overdue.

risk.note: A rebuild is a bigger project with real cost; plan it with a redesign, not as a rush job.

prerequisites: A redesign already planned, or the theme clearly costing more to patch than rebuild
steps: Compare the cost of continued patching against a rebuild on a simple base theme.
If a redesign is already planned, use it as the moment to rebuild rather than patch.
Benchmark two theme candidates on the same content and app embeds before committing.
Only choose a premium theme when a specific feature is known to make money.

test.method: Benchmark the new theme against the old one with identical content and embeds off.
test.read_point: Before launch, on published theme previews

title: Work only on a duplicate theme or staging site, and change one thing at a time
hypothesis: If every speed change happens on a duplicate theme or staging with a kept backup, then a broken change can be reverted without cost, because a live-site mistake is far more expensive than a staging one.

signal.check: Speed changes are being made directly on the live theme or live site with no backup or duplicate.

risk.note: This is itself the risk-reduction practice.

prerequisites: Ability to duplicate the theme or set up staging
steps: Duplicate the live theme (Shopify) or set up staging (WordPress) before any change.
Keep a labeled backup of the original.
Make one change, test it, then make the next.
Compare preview to preview, or staging to staging, never preview to live.

test.method: Confirm each change was made and tested on the duplicate or staging copy first.
test.read_point: Before publishing any change to the live site

title: For a single hero-SKU store, put nearly all speed effort into that one product page
hypothesis: If a store sells mostly one hero product, then focusing speed effort on that single PDP moves more revenue than spreading effort across a catalog that barely gets visited.
does_not_apply_when: Store has a large catalog with broadly spread traffic

signal.check: One product page accounts for most sessions and revenue, and speed effort has been spread evenly across the catalog instead.

risk.note: A prioritization decision.

prerequisites: Sessions and revenue by template
steps: Confirm the single hero SKU carries most sessions and revenue.
Run the full speed fix list (images, LCP, CLS, apps) on that one PDP first.
Skip catalog-wide compression work until the hero PDP is fully fixed.
Only extend to other pages once the hero PDP passes its thresholds.

test.method: Track conversion and bounce on the hero PDP before and after.

title: Let a high-AOV or luxury store keep a heavier hero image if LCP still passes
hypothesis: If a high-AOV or considered-purchase store keeps a richer hero image while LCP still passes the 2.5 second target, then it keeps its visual quality without a real speed cost, because the LCP threshold is what matters, not the file size alone.
does_not_apply_when: Low-AOV, high-volume, impulse-purchase stores, which should hold to the strict image size ceilings

signal.check: The store has a rich hero image and LCP is measured above 2.5 seconds, or the store is unsure how far it can push image quality.

expected_effect.size: target 2.5 seconds or less regardless of file size chosen

risk.note: A quality-vs-speed judgment call; test LCP after any change.

prerequisites: Store's own AOV band known
steps: Confirm the store is high-AOV, luxury or a considered purchase.
Set the target as LCP under 2.5 seconds rather than a strict file size ceiling.
Compress and preload the hero image only as far as needed to hit that LCP target.
Re-test LCP after every image change.

test.method: Measure LCP with the chosen hero image quality.

title: Sell speed work as a conversion and bounce fix, not a guaranteed ranking boost
hypothesis: If speed work is framed as a tie-breaker for ranking and a real fix for bounce and conversion, then the business case stays honest, because Core Web Vitals are one ranking signal among many, not a guarantee.

signal.check: A speed proposal promises a ranking increase as the main benefit, without mentioning conversion or bounce.

expected_effect.size: about 12% per second, per one source's benchmark

risk.note: A framing and honesty check, not a technical change.

steps: Describe Core Web Vitals as a ranking tie-breaker between pages of similar content quality.
Lead the business case with bounce rate and conversion rate, which speed reliably affects.
Never promise a specific ranking position gain from a speed fix.
Let content depth and other SEO work carry the ranking argument.

test.method: Check any client-facing speed report for ranking promises before it goes out.

title: Test the ad landing page and top product page inside in-app browsers, not only Safari or Chrome
hypothesis: If we test the ad landing page inside Instagram, TikTok and Facebook's own in-app browser, then we catch rendering or speed problems that most paid social clicks actually see, because those in-app browsers render differently from a normal mobile browser.
does_not_apply_when: Store runs no paid social ads

signal.check: The store runs paid social ads and speed testing has only used a normal mobile browser, never the platform's in-app browser.

risk.note: A testing step, not a change.

prerequisites: Store runs paid social campaigns
steps: Click through from an actual Instagram, TikTok or Facebook ad on a phone to open the in-app browser.
Load the ad landing page and watch for slow paint, layout shift or missing content.
Compare what you see to the same page in mobile Safari or Chrome.
Flag any gap between the two for a developer to investigate.

test.method: Repeat the in-app browser check after any landing page speed fix.

title: Check that currency conversion and geolocation redirects do not delay first paint
hypothesis: If we check that currency conversion and country redirects run without blocking the first paint, then shoppers in other countries or currencies do not face an extra delay before the page even starts.
does_not_apply_when: Single-country, single-currency stores

signal.check: The store sells in more than one country or currency and has never checked whether the redirect or currency-detection script blocks first paint.

risk.note: A check first; any fix should be tested on staging.

prerequisites: Store sells in multiple countries or currencies
steps: Load the store from a location or IP outside the home market.
Watch the Network panel for a redirect or currency-detection request before the page starts rendering.
If it blocks first paint, ask a developer to make it non-blocking or run it after first paint.
Re-test from more than one country if the store sells widely.

test.method: Measure TTFB and LCP from a non-home-market location before and after.

title: Average 3 test runs per page and wait before retesting after a change
hypothesis: If we run 3 tests per page and device and average them, waiting 1 to 2 minutes after a change before retesting, then we compare real gains instead of noise, because a single run can swing several points on its own.

signal.check: Speed comparisons are being made from a single test run, or immediately after a change with no wait.

expected_effect.size: one page scored 48, 51 and 54 across 3 runs in a row, per one source

risk.note: A testing practice, no site risk.

prerequisites: SPD-001 baseline done
steps: For every page and device that carries money, run the test 3 times.
Wait 1 to 2 minutes after any change before retesting.
Average the 3 runs and compare averages, not single readings.
Treat differences of a few points as noise, not a real change.

test.method: Log all 3 runs and the average in the change log for every comparison.
test.read_point: Every time a before/after comparison is made

title: Test every template type, not only the home page
hypothesis: If we test home, collection, product, cart and checkout separately, then we catch slow templates that a home-page-only test hides, because each template loads a different set of apps and images.

signal.check: Speed testing or reporting only covers the home page, or 'Core Web Vitals passed' is being read as a whole-store pass.

expected_effect.size: one store passed vitals on home while scoring 18 on home, 38 on collection and lower on product, per one source's case

risk.note: A test-coverage practice, not a site change.

prerequisites: SPD-001 baseline done
steps: Test home, a collection, a top product page, cart and checkout separately.
Test every distinct template design, not just one example of each page type.
Do not treat a passing home page score as a store-wide pass.

test.method: Compare vitals across all 5 core templates, not just home.

title: Read field and lab speed data as two different things, and fix from lab first
hypothesis: If we fix against lab data now and expect field data to confirm the gain in about 28 days, then we do not mistake a lag for a failed fix, because field data is a rolling 28-day window of real users.

signal.check: A fix was made recently and field Core Web Vitals in Search Console or PageSpeed Insights still show the old numbers.

expected_effect.size: one case moved 0.73, 0.66, 0.13, 0.1, 0 over about 28 days after the fix

risk.note: A reading discipline, not a change.

steps: Read the PSI top section as field data (real users, 28-day window) and the bottom as lab data (simulated).
If the URL toggle is greyed out from too little traffic, read Origin as a site-wide signal only.
Optimize against lab data now.
Wait about 28 days before judging the fix from field data or Search Console.

test.method: Track the same field metric weekly for 4 weeks after a fix.

title: Report only LCP, INP and CLS as the vitals that count, and drop retired metrics
hypothesis: If every speed report names LCP, INP and CLS as the vitals and treats FCP, TTFB, TBT and Speed Index as diagnostics, then targets stay aligned with what Google actually measures, because FID and TTI are retired.

signal.check: A report, target sheet or old audit still names FID, TTI, or calls TTFB or 'fully loaded time' a Core Web Vital.

risk.note: A reporting correction.

steps: Verify the current Core Web Vitals list at web.dev/articles/vitals before writing a report.
Use LCP, INP and CLS as the vitals in every deliverable.
List FCP, TTFB, TBT and Speed Index as diagnostics, not vitals.
Remove FID and TTI from any template or target sheet still using them.

test.method: Check any speed report or brief for retired metric names before it goes out.

title: Run a slow-connection visual test on the ad landing page and top product page
hypothesis: If we throttle the connection and watch the page load by eye, then we catch hidden heroes, blank waits and layout jumps that a good score can miss, because a shopper on a real slow connection feels these even when the lab score looks fine.

signal.check: A page has a passing PSI score but has never been watched loading on a throttled slow-4G or 3G connection.

risk.note: A test-only step.

steps: Open Chrome DevTools Network tab, tick Disable cache.
Throttle to Slow 4G or 3G, whichever matches the store's real visitor connections.
Reload and watch: time to first content, layout jumps, images revealing in chunks, a hidden main image.
If needed, add a custom slower profile (about 20 kbps) to catch subtle shifts.
Repeat after each fix stage so gains can be attributed.

test.method: Repeat the throttled visual test before and after a fix and note the difference in words.

title: Confirm a speed test actually saw your latest change before trusting the result
hypothesis: If we place a visible marker above the fold and confirm it shows in the test screenshot, then we avoid wrongly concluding a fix did not work when the test actually just served a cached page.

signal.check: A retest right after a change shows no improvement, and no one confirmed the test saw the new page version.

risk.note: Add and remove a text marker; no lasting change.

steps: Add a small visible line of text above the fold as a marker.
Rerun PageSpeed Insights and check the screenshot for the marker.
If the marker is missing, clear theme, plugin or CDN caches and rerun.
Remove the marker once confirmed.
On Shopify, also wait 1 to 2 minutes after saving before the retest.

test.method: Check the PSI screenshot for the marker on every retest.

title: Cross-check a suspicious speed result with a second tool
hypothesis: If we confirm a finding with GTmetrix or WebPageTest when PageSpeed Insights runs out or looks odd, then we trust findings both tools agree on first, because each tool defines 'loaded' differently and scores cannot be compared across tools.

signal.check: PageSpeed Insights is unavailable, rate-limited, or gives a result that looks inconsistent with what the site feels like.

risk.note: A verification step.

steps: Run the same URL through GTmetrix or WebPageTest.
Compare the waterfall or filmstrip, not the numeric score, across tools.
Fix findings both tools flag first.
Never compare raw scores between PageSpeed Insights, GTmetrix and WebPageTest.

test.method: Note agreement or disagreement between the two tools for each finding.
test.read_point: Whenever a second opinion is needed

title: Crawl every page of a large catalog for speed outliers instead of sampling
hypothesis: If we run a site-wide crawl across hundreds of URLs, then we find the small number of outlier slow pages that a spot-check would miss, because slow pages hide in a large catalog.
does_not_apply_when: Small catalogs of a few dozen pages or fewer

signal.check: The store has hundreds of product or category pages and speed testing has only checked a handful of them.

risk.note: Running against production can load the server hard; use staging or throttle the crawl.

prerequisites: Node.js available
Staging URL, or owner's go-ahead to crawl production
steps: Run `npx unlighthouse --site <url>` against staging where possible.
Sort results by score and list the outlier pages and their templates.
Confirm the worst pages with PageSpeed Insights field data.
Optionally add the Unlighthouse SDK to CI to keep the check running.

test.method: Compare outlier count and severity before and after fixing the flagged templates.

title: Clear the Chrome Lighthouse list before chasing PageSpeed Insights' longer list
hypothesis: If we fix the shorter Lighthouse list in Chrome DevTools first, then PageSpeed Insights' remaining list becomes clearer and more actionable, because Lighthouse surfaces fewer, sharper issues on Shopify stores.

signal.check: A Shopify audit is working from PageSpeed Insights' full list without first checking Chrome DevTools Lighthouse.

risk.note: A sequencing choice, not a change.

steps: Right-click the page, Inspect, open the Lighthouse tab, Analyze page load.
Fix the issues Lighthouse flags first.
Move to PageSpeed Insights' list next.
Expect new items to surface as old ones clear; keep iterating.

test.method: Re-run both tools after the Lighthouse-first pass.

title: Test checkout speed as its own check, separate from the site-wide score
hypothesis: If we test the checkout flow on its own, then we catch slow payment, address and fraud scripts that a home or product page score never shows, because site-wide scores skip checkout.

signal.check: Speed audits stop at product or cart pages and never load or time the checkout flow itself.

risk.note: A test-only step.

steps: Walk the full checkout flow on a phone: address, shipping, payment.
Watch for any step that feels slow, especially cart total calculation and fraud checks.
Note timing separately from the home or product page score.

test.method: Time each checkout step by feel and by Network panel waterfall.

title: Change one script or setting at a time and retest before the next change
hypothesis: If we change only one setting or script at a time and retest the cart, add-to-cart and tracking after each, then a broken feature is easy to trace, because a batch of changes hides which one caused it.

signal.check: A planned speed fix bundles several script removals or setting changes into one deployment.

risk.note: A process discipline that reduces risk rather than adding it.

prerequisites: SPD-014 duplicate theme or staging in use
steps: Make one JS minify, defer, delay or removal change at a time.
Browse the live or staging site in incognito after each change.
Test cart, add-to-cart and tracking before making the next change.
If something breaks, you now know exactly which change did it.

test.method: Confirm cart, add-to-cart and tracking work after each single change.

title: Wait about 28 days of field data before judging whether a fix worked
hypothesis: If we wait about 28 days before reading Search Console or the PageSpeed Insights history graph, then we avoid calling a real fix a failure too early, because CrUX field data is a rolling 28-day window.

signal.check: A fix shipped less than 28 days ago and someone is already judging it a failure from field data or Search Console.

expected_effect.size: field lag observed at 'a couple of days' to about 28 days in different cases

risk.note: A patience rule, not a change.

steps: Note the fix date in the change log.
Set a reminder for 28 days out to check field data and Search Console.
Do not conclude a fix failed from field data read before that date.

test.method: Compare field metrics at day 0, day 14 and day 28.

title: Measure third-party script weight from response headers, not the browser's timing API
hypothesis: If we sum compressed sizes from response headers or a direct fetch, then third-party byte totals are accurate, because the browser's Resource Timing API reports 0 bytes for most cross-origin scripts and can be 4x too low.

signal.check: A third-party byte total was pulled from the browser's Resource Timing API or from decoded (uncompressed) sizes.

expected_effect.size: one audit found the true figure was 470 KB where the two flawed methods gave 110 KB and 1.05 MB

risk.note: A measurement correction.

steps: Open DevTools Network or the CDP log and read compressed response sizes directly from headers.
Or fetch each third-party script directly with Accept-Encoding: br, gzip and sum the sizes.
Do not use the Resource Timing API for cross-origin script sizes.
Report the corrected total, and say which method was used.

test.method: Compare the corrected total against a Resource Timing API reading to show the gap.

title: Check images first, and do not trust automatic platform compression alone
hypothesis: If we check images before anything else and treat platform auto-compression as a floor, not a fix, then we catch the biggest single weight on the page, because platform compression alone was not enough in a documented case.

signal.check: The store believes the platform's automatic image handling makes manual image work unnecessary, and images have never been checked directly.

expected_effect.size: a 9.8 MB upload was still delivered at 6.1 MB by platform compression alone, per one source

risk.note: A diagnostic step.

steps: Check the delivered file size of the largest images on the busiest pages.
Do not assume the platform's own compression is enough just because it exists.
Prioritize images first when the theme is old or custom-built, the catalog is large, or mobile share is high.

test.method: Compare delivered image size against the ceilings in SPD-036.

title: Resize images to about 2,000 px before upload instead of shipping camera-size originals
hypothesis: If we resize the long edge to about 2,000 px before upload, capping full-bleed heroes at 3,000 px, then file weight drops sharply, because a camera photo can exceed 5 MB while 2,000 px is enough for zoom and retina.

signal.check: Product or section images were uploaded straight from a camera, phone or design tool without resizing first.

expected_effect.size: a 4,000 x 3,000 camera photo can exceed 5 MB; resized examples reached 46 KB at 1,920 px

risk.note: Keep the original file; resizing is easy to redo.

steps: Batch-resize same-orientation images to a long edge of about 2,000 px.
Use up to 3,000 px only for a full-bleed hero image.
Never upload a raw camera, DSLR or design-tool original.
Keep the original file before resizing.

test.method: Compare file size before and after resizing on a sample of images.

title: Export and serve each image near its real display size
hypothesis: If we export images at about 2x their rendered width, capped at 2,000 px, then no page ships a 6 MB image for a 700 px box, because oversized intrinsic dimensions waste bandwidth with no visible gain.

signal.check: An image's intrinsic width is more than about 2x its rendered box width on the page.

expected_effect.size: example flagged: a 5,000 px image in a 700 px box at 6 MB

risk.note: Keep the original; re-export is easy to redo.

steps: Inspect an image on the live page and hover its src to read intrinsic vs rendered size.
Export at about 2x the rendered width, never below the box width.
Never use the platform's master or original file URL directly on the page.
Flag and re-export any image whose intrinsic size is more than 2x its box.

test.method: Recheck the intrinsic-to-rendered ratio after re-export.

title: Hold hard file-size ceilings for product, hero and LCP images
hypothesis: If we set product images under 100 KB, hero images under 200 KB, the LCP image under 250 KB, and treat 500 KB as a hard stop for any image, then no single image can dominate page weight.

signal.check: Any product, hero or LCP image on the site is heavier than these ceilings.

expected_effect.size: product under 100 KB, hero under 200 KB, LCP image under 250 KB, hard stop 500 KB

risk.note: Keep the original; recompress if quality suffers.

steps: Check every product image against a 100 KB target.
Check every hero image against a 200 KB target.
Check the specific LCP image on each template against a 250 KB cap.
Treat 500 KB as the hard stop for any image on any page.
Report which images exceed each line separately.

test.method: Audit file sizes in Content > Files or the media library against the ceilings.

title: Use the right image format for the job: JPEG for photos, PNG only for transparency, never GIF
hypothesis: If we export photos as JPEG, reserve PNG for images that need transparency, and replace GIFs with MP4, then file weight drops, because a photo saved as PNG can balloon from 2.7 MB to 8 MB.

signal.check: A photo is saved as PNG with no transparency need, or an animated GIF is used anywhere on the site.

expected_effect.size: a photo re-exported as PNG went from 2.7 MB to 8 MB, per one source

risk.note: A file format swap; keep the original.

steps: Find any photo saved as PNG and re-export as JPEG.
Confirm PNG is used only where transparency is needed.
Replace any animated GIF with an MP4 video.

test.method: Compare file size before and after the format swap.

title: Let the platform or CDN deliver WebP or AVIF instead of hand-uploading next-gen formats
hypothesis: If we upload JPEG or PNG and let the platform or CDN convert to WebP or AVIF automatically, then browsers that do not support the newer format still get a working image, because hand-uploaded WebP on some platforms can show nothing to unsupported browsers.
does_not_apply_when: Self-hosted stores that control image delivery directly, like WordPress, where exporting AVIF or WebP by hand fits

signal.check: WebP or AVIF files were uploaded by hand to a platform that already auto-converts images.

expected_effect.size: WebP is 25% to 35% smaller than JPEG at equal quality; WebP or AVIF 30% to 50% smaller overall

risk.note: A delivery choice, not a destructive change.

steps: Confirm whether the platform auto-serves WebP or AVIF with a JPEG or PNG fallback.
If it does, upload JPEG or PNG only and let the platform convert.
On self-hosted stores, export AVIF at about 50% quality or WebP directly, with a fallback.

test.method: Check the Network panel for the delivered image format on modern vs older browsers.

title: Compress every image once from the original, stopping just before visible quality loss
hypothesis: If we compress from the original file once at about 70 to 80% JPEG quality (or about 50% for AVIF), then file weight drops sharply without a visible quality loss on the product, because repeat compression degrades quality for little gain.

signal.check: Images have been compressed more than once, or compression quality was never checked against a visual preview.

expected_effect.size: one example dropped from 2.7 MB to 172 KB at quality 40; a second compression pass on an already-compressed file saved only 8%

risk.note: Keep the original file so compression can be redone.

steps: Keep the original, uncompressed file.
Compress from the original at about JPEG 70 to 80% quality (AVIF about 50%) using a visual preview.
Stop lowering quality just before the shopper would notice a difference on the item they are buying.
Do not run a second compression pass on an already-compressed file.

test.method: Compare file size and a visual preview before and after compression.

title: Make the theme serve responsive image widths instead of one master file
hypothesis: If the theme serves several image widths (srcset or width variants) instead of one master URL, then small screens stop downloading a full-size image, because a single master src ignores viewport size entirely.

signal.check: A theme section renders an image with a single src using the master file URL instead of srcset or width variants.

risk.note: Theme code change; test on staging and check every breakpoint.

prerequisites: Access to theme code, or a developer brief
steps: Open the theme section or snippet that renders the image.
Check whether it uses a single src with the master URL, which is the bad pattern.
Replace with srcset or several width variants (for example 1,600 default, 800 under 800 px, 1,200 under 1,200 px).
Use thumbnails, never full-size photos, in category grids.
Check every image-rendering section on old, custom or agency-built themes.
Hand to a developer if the theme is complex.

test.method: Check delivered image width in the Network panel at several viewport sizes.
test.read_point: After the theme change, on mobile and desktop

title: Lazy-load every image below the fold
hypothesis: If every image below the fold gets loading='lazy', then the browser stops downloading images the shopper has not scrolled to yet, because browsers otherwise fetch every image on the page at once.

signal.check: The Network panel shows every image on a page downloading at once on load, including footer, related-product and review images.

risk.note: Safe when applied only below the fold; never on in-view images (see SPD-042).

steps: Add loading='lazy' to every image not visible at first load, including footer logos.
Include slides 2 and on in any carousel, social feeds and related-product images.
Verify in the Network panel that below-fold images only load on scroll.

test.method: Watch the Network panel on load and confirm only in-view images download immediately.

title: Force eager loading on hero, logo and first-card images a plugin might lazy-load by default
hypothesis: If we explicitly set loading='eager' on hero, logo, first slide, main product image and the first grid card, then LCP does not suffer, because a theme section or plugin can lazy-load these by default even though they are visible at once.

signal.check: The hero, logo, first slide or first grid card carries loading='lazy' or a lazyload class even though it is visible without scrolling.

expected_effect.size: lazy-loading an in-view image 'actually hurts LCP' per one source

risk.note: Attribute change only.

steps: Inspect the hero, logo, first slide, main product image and first grid card.
Set loading='eager' explicitly, since the attribute only works on , not CSS backgrounds.
For a grid loop, set the first item eager and every other item lazy.
Re-check after any theme or plugin update, since defaults can reset.

test.method: Inspect the element and confirm loading='eager' is present after any theme update.
test.read_point: After the change and after any future theme update

title: Preload only the LCP image, with high fetch priority
hypothesis: If we add a preload with fetchpriority='high' for the LCP image only, and low priority far down the page, then the LCP element starts downloading sooner without creating contention, because too many preloads recreate the problem they were meant to fix.

signal.check: The LCP image has no preload tag, or several assets are preloaded at once.

expected_effect.size: one case moved from about 43-50 with preload alone to 50-60 combined with other fixes

risk.note: Check current browser support for the syntax before relying on it.

steps: Identify the LCP element per template (P18, P79).
Add <link rel='preload'> with fetchpriority='high' for that image only.
On product pages, add logic so the right image preloads per product.
Set fetchpriority='low' on images far down the page.
Do not preload more than the LCP image and critical fonts.

test.method: Measure LCP before and after adding the preload.

title: Add width, height or aspect-ratio to every image and video in normal page flow
hypothesis: If every image and video carries width and height attributes or a CSS aspect-ratio, then the layout stops jumping as media loads, because a jump right before a tap can push it away from Add to Cart.

signal.check: Product, grid or cart-thumbnail images are missing width, height or an aspect-ratio rule, and the page visibly jumps as they load.

expected_effect.size: unknown, depends on how many elements lack dimensions

risk.note: Attribute or CSS addition.

steps: Inspect PDP, grid and cart-thumbnail images for missing width and height.
Add numeric width and height attributes, or a CSS aspect-ratio rule kept by the surrounding CSS.
For responsive images whose ratio changes by viewport, use srcset instead.
On WordPress, use a plugin's 'Add missing width and height attributes' feature as a quick fix.

test.method: Watch the page load on a throttled connection and confirm no jump around the fixed elements.

title: Automate image compression for large catalogs, and verify it covers non-product images too
hypothesis: If we automate compression for a large catalog and then check that section and home page images are covered too, then no heavy image is missed, because bulk apps often touch only product images and leave section images at several MB.
does_not_apply_when: Small catalogs where manual compression is manageable

signal.check: The store has hundreds of SKUs or more, and a bulk compression app has run but section and home page images have not been checked separately.

risk.note: Measure before and after, since the compression app adds its own scripts.

steps: Install a bulk compression app set to compress on upload, or use a CDN image service at very high SKU counts.
Measure page weight before and after running it, since the app adds its own scripts.
Separately check Content > Files or the media library for section and home page images the app skipped.
Keep the manual pipeline for hero and launch images.

test.method: Sample product and non-product images after the bulk run and check both are under the size ceilings.

title: Use one strong hero instead of a heavy auto-rotating slider
hypothesis: If we replace a 4-to-5-slide auto-rotating slider with one strong hero, or at most 2 to 3 static slides, then the home or collection page loads far less image weight, because auto-rotating sliders load every slide up front.

signal.check: The home page or a collection banner uses an auto-rotating slider with 4 or more slides.

expected_effect.size: unknown, depends on slide count and size

risk.note: A content and layout change; confirm the owner is fine with fewer slides.

steps: Count current slides and their file sizes.
Replace with 1 strong hero image and a clear call to action, or at most 2 to 3 static slides.
Make slide 1 eager and any remaining slides lazy.
Use srcset on each slide.

test.method: Compare page weight and LCP before and after cutting slide count.

title: Check the file library for multi-MB non-product images every audit
hypothesis: If we check Content > Files or the media library directly for oversized section, banner and background images, then heavy files get caught, because bulk compressor apps often only touch product images.

signal.check: The file or media library has never been sorted by size, and a bulk compressor app runs on products only.

expected_effect.size: examples found at 3 MB and 5 MB per file

risk.note: Keep the original file before recompressing.

steps: Open Content > Files or the media library and sort by file size.
Flag anything over the 500 KB hard stop.
Find the section using each heavy image and download it.
Resize and compress, then re-upload in place of the original.

test.method: Re-check the sorted file list after the sweep.

title: Use one media file per image and Replace to update it, instead of re-uploading
hypothesis: If we keep one file per image and use Replace to update it everywhere it is used, then the library stays clean and every placement gets the fix, because uploading the same file twice creates a second URL that needs its own edits.

signal.check: The media library has duplicate files with the same content under different names or suffixes.

risk.note: A housekeeping task.

steps: Search the media library for duplicate file names or gibberish suffixes.
Pick one canonical file per image and delete the duplicates.
Use Replace image to update a file everywhere it is placed, and check each placement after.

test.method: Search the library again after cleanup to confirm no duplicates remain.

title: Combine small icons into one sprite instead of many separate image requests
hypothesis: If we combine small repeated icons into a single sprite sheet, then the page makes fewer requests, because each separate small icon file adds its own round trip.

signal.check: Several small icons (payment badges, social icons, trust badges) each load as a separate image file.

risk.note: A code change; test the icons still display correctly.

prerequisites: Developer or theme code access
steps: List every small repeated icon on the page.
Combine them into one sprite sheet image or an inline SVG set.
Update the theme code to reference the sprite instead of individual files.
Verify every icon still displays correctly at each size.

test.method: Count image requests before and after in the Network panel.

title: Search the theme for and remove empty image src attributes
hypothesis: If we remove every empty img src attribute, then those wasted requests stop, because src='' still sends a request even with nothing to load.

signal.check: A search of the theme code finds img tags with an empty src attribute, often left by pasted builder settings.

risk.note: A small code cleanup.

steps: Search the theme code for src=''.
Remove or fix each occurrence.
Re-check the page after the fix to confirm no broken images appear.

test.method: Search the theme again after the cleanup.

title: Crop images one at a time instead of in bulk, to match each grid's aspect ratio
hypothesis: If we crop each image individually rather than in a bulk batch, then every image fits its grid at the intended ratio, because product position differs per shot and bulk cropping produces mixed aspect ratios that also risk layout shift.

signal.check: A collection grid shows images at inconsistent heights or aspect ratios because they were cropped in a bulk batch.

risk.note: Keep originals; re-crop is easy to redo.

steps: Identify grids with mixed image aspect ratios.
Crop each image individually to the grid's target ratio, such as square for general grids or 4:5 for fashion.
Do not bulk-crop a folder of mixed-orientation shots in one pass.

test.method: Visually check the grid for consistent heights after cropping.

title: Run a sweep to find and fix heavy images already live on the store
hypothesis: If we run a fixed download-compress-resize-reupload loop on every image already over the size ceiling, then legacy heavy images get cleared out, not just new uploads going forward.

signal.check: The store has been live for a while and has never done a full sweep of existing images against the current size ceilings.

expected_effect.size: one example cut a 1.7 MB image to about 400 KB after resize and a second compression pass

risk.note: Keep original files.

prerequisites: SPD-047 file library sweep done
steps: List every image over the size ceiling found in the file library sweep.
Download each one, compress it, and resize if still over budget.
Compress again after resizing if needed.
Re-upload in place of the original and verify the placement.

test.method: Re-check file sizes against the ceilings after the sweep.

title: Inventory every route a script uses to reach the page before touching any of them
hypothesis: If we list which of the 3 routes (Shopify's async injection, hardcoded script tags, or app embeds) each script uses, then later delay or removal work targets the right mechanism, because each route needs a different fix.
does_not_apply_when: WordPress and other self-hosted stores, which should read the GTmetrix waterfall and PSI render-blocking list instead

signal.check: A script triage is starting and no one has separated scripts by how they reach the page.

risk.note: A read-only inventory step.

steps: In DevTools Elements, expand the head and find the async load function inside content_for_header; list every app script URL it injects.
Search theme.liquid for hardcoded <script> tags pasted by hand.
Check Customize > App embeds for scripts added there.
Record which route each script uses before deciding what to do with it.

test.method: Confirm the inventory lists every script found in the head by any route.

title: Search for and remove residual app code after every uninstall
hypothesis: If we search the theme for an app's brand name and App Store listing name after uninstalling it, then leftover scripts stop calling external servers on every page view, because uninstalling an app does not clean the theme by itself.

signal.check: An app was uninstalled recently and no one searched the theme code for its leftover script tags, JS, CSS or snippets.

risk.note: Only remove code for apps actually uninstalled; do not touch scripts you cannot identify.

prerequisites: Backup or duplicate theme
steps: Search theme.liquid, head and footer snippets for the app's brand name and its App Store listing name, since they can differ.
Deep-search by downloading the theme file and searching all files, including JSON files.
Remove or comment out only the identified tag.
Scroll theme.liquid for any other unrecognized script or pixel tag and check it against installed apps before touching it.
Save, load the store, and confirm it still works.
Re-test after each removal so effects can be attributed.

test.method: Search again for the app's name after removal to confirm no hits remain.

title: Vet a new app before installing it: reviews, existing features, and a before-and-after test
hypothesis: If we check reviews for speed complaints, confirm the theme does not already do the job, and run a before-and-after speed test on any new app, then the store avoids adding weight it did not need to add.

signal.check: A new app or plugin is about to be installed and no speed vetting has happened yet.

risk.note: A vetting step before install; low risk by design.

steps: Check the app's reviews for speed complaints.
Confirm the theme does not already offer this feature.
Run a speed test before installing.
Install, then run the same speed test again and compare.

test.method: Compare the before and after speed test for every new install, for the life of the store.

title: Add defer to blocking scripts, fall back to async, and test the exact feature they power
hypothesis: If we add defer first to a blocking script and fall back to async only if defer breaks it, then non-critical scripts stop blocking render while dependent scripts keep their order, because defer preserves order and async does not.

signal.check: PSI or Lighthouse's render-blocking list shows a script tag with neither defer nor async.

expected_effect.size: one example moved 78 to 80 after a single defer

risk.note: Test the exact feature the script powers before and after; revert if it breaks.

prerequisites: SPD-053 script inventory done
steps: Identify what each blocking script does and which app it belongs to; skip anything unidentified.
Add defer to the script tag and save.
Load the store and test the exact feature the script powers.
If it breaks, try async instead and test again; if that also breaks, remove the attribute and leave it blocking.
Re-run Lighthouse to confirm the render-blocking entry is gone.

test.method: Function-test the specific feature (reviews, upsell, chat) after each attribute change, then re-run Lighthouse.

title: Delay non-critical widget scripts until the shopper's first interaction
hypothesis: If loyalty, chat, cookie banner, social feed and upsell-drawer scripts wait until the first scroll, click or key press, then initial load gets lighter, because these widgets are not needed until the shopper starts engaging.
does_not_apply_when: Widgets that must show at first paint, such as above-the-fold review stars; payment and fraud scripts; tracking pixels

signal.check: Chat, loyalty, social feed or upsell-drawer scripts load at first paint even though they sit below the fold or outside the buying flow.

expected_effect.size: 10 to 20% score gain claimed when apps are the bottleneck; small when CLS or LCP dominate

risk.note: Test every delayed app's full function and every tracking event before calling it done.

prerequisites: Which widgets must show at first paint
CLS and LCP fixed or at least measured first
steps: List which widgets are not in view and not part of the buying flow.
Confirm none of them are payment, fraud, or pixel scripts, which should not be delayed this way.
Delay each one to first scroll, click, mousemove or key press.
Exercise every delayed app's full function before calling it done.

test.method: Load the page fresh, confirm widgets are absent, then interact and confirm they appear and work.

title: On Shopify, delay every non-critical app script at once via the content_for_header override
hypothesis: If a developer wraps content_for_header and replays it on first interaction, then every non-critical app script delays at once, because this is the single injection point Shopify uses for nearly all app scripts.

signal.check: Many app scripts inject through content_for_header and no delay mechanism exists yet.

expected_effect.size: 10 to 20% claimed when apps are the bottleneck

risk.note: Can break tracking, reviews or checkout-adjacent widgets if not tested fully; never comment out content_for_header directly.

prerequisites: SPD-057 concept agreed
Duplicate theme
steps: Copy the list of app script URLs from the async load function for the record.
Wrap content_for_header in a comment block and render a snippet beside it that replays it on first interaction.
Verify: on refresh with no interaction, widgets are absent; on mouse move, a console message fires and widgets appear.
Exercise every app fully: reviews, upsells, loyalty, forms, chat, subscriptions.
Test tracking events with consent accepted and refused; if events break, keep pixels in the initial load.

test.method: Function-test every app and every tracking event with consent on and off before and after.

title: On Shopify, delay one specific app script by capturing and filtering it out of content_for_header
hypothesis: If we capture content_for_header, strip out one app's script URL, and re-inject it on first interaction, then that single app delays without touching every other script, giving a safer, narrower change than delaying everything at once.

signal.check: One specific app is identified as a delay candidate, but a full content_for_header override is too risky to do all at once.

risk.note: If the app still works after removal, it is also injected via an app embed; toggle that off too.

prerequisites: Target app's script URL identified
steps: Copy the app's script URL from the async load function.
In theme.liquid, capture content_for_header, assign a version with that URL removed, and output the modified version.
Confirm the app stops working on the front end; if it still works, toggle its app embed off too.
Create a snippet that injects the script on first interaction and render it in theme.liquid.
Verify the app fires and works on click or scroll.

test.method: Confirm the app is absent at load and fires correctly on first interaction.

title: On Shopify, delay an app-embed widget's script and stylesheet until first interaction
hypothesis: If we add an app embed's JS and CSS URLs to a lazy-load list and toggle the embed off in Customize, then a chat or similar embed widget stops loading at first paint, because embeds inject straight into the head by default.

signal.check: An app embed widget such as chat loads at first paint even though it is not part of the buying flow.

expected_effect.size: one example moved from 57 to about 65

risk.note: Re-check after app updates, since script URLs can change.

steps: With the embed on, find its script and CSS URLs via DevTools Elements, Edit as HTML.
Add both URLs to the lazy-load function's list.
Toggle the app off in Customize > App embeds and save.
Verify the widget appears only after hover or scroll and works fully.
Re-check after any app update, since URLs can change.

test.method: Load the page fresh and confirm the widget is absent, then interact and confirm it appears.
test.read_point: After deployment and after any future app update

title: Delay a hardcoded script, such as a cookie banner, only with a documented compliance go-ahead
lever: hardcoded script delay with compliance check
hypothesis: If we delay a hardcoded cookie-banner script to first interaction only after confirming the store's consent rules allow it, then we cut its layout shift and blocking without a legal problem.
does_not_apply_when: Markets where consent rules require the banner to show immediately, without a documented go-ahead first

signal.check: A cookie or consent banner is hardcoded in theme.liquid and causes layout shift or blocking time, and the store's consent rules by market have not been checked.

expected_effect.size: one case moved score 48 to 57 with CLS gone

risk.note: Get a documented go-ahead from whoever owns compliance before delaying a consent banner.

prerequisites: Consent rules for the store's markets confirmed
Written go-ahead from whoever owns compliance
steps: Confirm the banner is the cause of CLS or blocking in the report.
Get written confirmation that delaying it is allowed for the store's markets.
Comment out the script tag and paste the lazy-load function with the banner's URL before </head>.
Verify: on refresh, the banner is absent; on mouse move, it appears with a console message.

test.method: Confirm the banner appears on first interaction and CLS drops on the throttled test.

title: Never change how tracking pixels load without testing every event with consent on and off
hypothesis: If we test page view, variant, add-to-cart and a test purchase event before and after any pixel or tag-manager change, with consent accepted and refused, then a speed fix does not quietly break tracking data.

signal.check: A defer, delay or tag manager change is planned that touches how a tracking pixel loads, and no event test plan exists.

risk.note: A broken pixel can silently corrupt weeks of ad data before anyone notices.

steps: Before the change, record baseline event firing for page view, variant, add-to-cart and a test purchase.
Make the change on staging.
Retest the same events with consent accepted and with consent refused.
Check for missing and duplicated events; keep the pixel in initial load if events break.
Only publish once every event fires correctly.

test.method: Compare event counts before and after in the pixel's own event manager or debug tool.

title: Load an app's assets only on the templates where its widget actually appears
hypothesis: If reviews and subscription scripts load only on collection and product pages, rewards scripts only on the rewards page, and carousel libraries only where a carousel appears, then unrelated pages stop carrying weight they never use.

signal.check: PSI's 'unused CSS' or 'unused JavaScript' flag names an app's assets on templates where its widget is not visible.

risk.note: Test each template after the change so a moved widget does not silently lose its assets.

prerequisites: Developer or theme code access for complex themes
steps: For each script flagged as unused on a template, check whether its widget is visible there.
Load those assets conditionally by template using Liquid template conditions or the equivalent.
Look for the same script loaded twice (for example, a pixel by hand and by an app) and remove the duplicate.
Test events and the widget's function on every affected template.

test.method: Re-check PSI's unused CSS/JS flag on the affected templates after the change.

title: Remove or self-host any library loaded from an outside CDN
hypothesis: If we remove jQuery or self-host any library the theme still needs, then a third-party CDN outage can no longer take down Add to Cart, because the library no longer depends on an external host.

signal.check: The theme loads jQuery or another JavaScript library from an outside CDN URL.

risk.note: Confirm the cart drawer and checkout do not still need the library before removing it.

steps: Check whether the cart drawer or checkout actually needs the library.
If not needed, remove it and use vanilla JavaScript instead.
If it is needed, download the file and upload it to the theme's own assets folder.
Reference it with asset_url instead of the outside CDN URL.
On WordPress, dequeue jQuery only for logged-out front-end visitors, since the admin bar needs it.

test.method: Confirm the cart drawer, add-to-cart and checkout still work after removing the outside CDN reference.

title: Turn off every Shopify app embed that is not actively used
hypothesis: If we turn off every app embed toggle that is not actively used, then those scripts stop loading straight into the head, because an embed left on for an uninstalled or unused app still injects code.

signal.check: Customize > App embeds shows a toggle on for an app that is uninstalled, unused, or whose feature is not visible on the store.

risk.note: Toggling an embed off is easy to reverse if a feature turns out to be needed.

steps: Open Customize > App embeds.
Turn off every embed not actively in use.
Save and re-check the store for any missing feature.
Re-check embeds again after every uninstall, since an uninstalled app's embed should disappear.

test.method: Confirm no needed feature broke after turning off unused embeds.

title: Never comment out content_for_header directly; use the supported delay method instead
hypothesis: If we always use the wrap-and-replay method for content_for_header instead of commenting it out on the live theme, then apps and platform features keep working, because commenting it out breaks apps and platform features outright.

signal.check: A developer or agent is tempted to comment out content_for_header directly to test a speed score, on a live theme.

expected_effect.size: one demo went from score 80 to 100 with it commented out, but this breaks apps and platform features

risk.note: Commenting it out on a live theme breaks apps and platform features; only ever test this on a duplicate theme, never live.

steps: Never comment out content_for_header on the live theme, even to see the score change.
If testing the effect, do it only on a duplicate theme, never live.
Use the supported wrap-and-replay method (SPD-058) instead of removing the block.

test.method: Confirm the live theme's content_for_header block is intact and unmodified except by the supported wrapper.
test.read_point: Any time this section of theme.liquid is touched

title: Load non-essential third parties after the product image and info, not before
hypothesis: If reviews, upsells and other non-essential integrations load after the main product image and description, then the shopper sees the buy box first, because payment and fraud scripts are the only integrations that may need to load earlier.

signal.check: A product page loads reviews, upsell widgets or social proof scripts ahead of the main image and product information.

risk.note: Check that analytics still fire correctly after reordering.

steps: Identify integrations loading ahead of the main image and product info on the product page.
Reorder or delay non-essential ones to load after the buy box.
Keep payment and fraud scripts loading early if they need to.
Check analytics events still fire after the reorder.

test.method: Watch the Network waterfall to confirm the buy box loads before non-essential integrations.

title: Use a tag manager for inventory and a kill switch, not as a speed fix
hypothesis: If we treat a tag manager as a way to inventory tags and quickly disable a failing one, then we stop expecting it to condense every vendor tag into one request, because that is not actually how a tag manager works.

signal.check: The store's tag manager is being credited with a speed improvement it did not measurably deliver.

expected_effect.size: unknown, a tag manager does not itself reduce script count

risk.note: An expectation correction.

steps: List every tag the tag manager fires.
Measure the waterfall to see the real request count and weight per tag.
Use the tag manager to disable a failing tag fast, not to expect it to cut request count on its own.

test.method: Confirm the waterfall, not the tag manager's own claims, drives the speed assessment.
test.read_point: Every audit involving many tracking tags

title: Test any speed or caching app like any other change before trusting it
hypothesis: If we test a speed app or caching script with the same before-and-after protocol as any other change, then we avoid paying for a tool that helps only returning users, if at all, because Shopify already caches and minifies theme assets.

signal.check: A 'speed' or 'caching' app or script is installed on Shopify with no measured before-and-after test, or a WordPress optimization plugin's settings were all turned on at once.

expected_effect.size: unknown, and may be zero on Shopify since caching is already handled

risk.note: Testing rather than trusting marketing claims.

steps: On Shopify, default to no speed app unless a specific measured gain justifies it.
On WordPress, use one optimization plugin, and test each setting one at a time (SPD-030).
Measure with the app's own scripts included in the total, since the app itself adds weight.
Remove any tool that does not show a measured gain.

test.method: Compare speed with the app on vs off, including its own script weight.

title: Add third-party script count to the store's speed budget as its own tracked number
hypothesis: If we track third-party script count as a leading number in the speed budget, then app creep gets caught early, because script count is a strong predictor of mobile score across a large benchmark dataset.

signal.check: The store's speed budget or monitoring setup does not track the number of distinct third-party scripts per page.

expected_effect.size: median mobile score 74 at 0-5 third-party services vs 44 at 21-30, in a 1,533-store dataset; more than 20 apps is a warning sign

risk.note: A tracking addition.

prerequisites: SPD-008 speed budget exists
steps: Count distinct third-party hosts on each key template's waterfall.
Add this count as a line in the speed budget alongside page weight and score.
Set a warning line at more than 20 apps.
Review any new app request against this number before approving it.

test.method: Track the script count over time alongside score and page weight.

title: Move compatible third-party scripts to a web worker at rebuild time
hypothesis: If we move compatible third-party scripts to a web worker such as Partytown during a rebuild, then they stop competing with the main thread, because main-thread JavaScript is what drives poor INP and TBT.
does_not_apply_when: Not every script is compatible with a worker; verify each one individually

signal.check: A store is doing a framework or headless rebuild and has several third-party scripts competing with the main thread.

risk.note: Test each moved script individually; not all scripts work correctly in a worker.

prerequisites: A framework or headless rebuild already underway
steps: List third-party scripts that are candidates for a worker.
Test each one individually in Partytown or an equivalent worker library.
Move only the scripts that work correctly.
Confirm tracking and interactive widgets still function after the move.

test.method: Compare INP and TBT before and after moving each script.

title: Check for CDN script rewriting before blaming the code when first-party JS runs late
hypothesis: If we check whether a CDN feature like Cloudflare Rocket Loader is rewriting and delaying first-party scripts, then we fix the real cause in 15 minutes, instead of debugging application code that was never the problem.

signal.check: First-party JavaScript only runs after the load event even though its chunks arrived earlier, and the store sits behind Cloudflare or a similar CDN.

expected_effect.size: found on one audit; fix took about 15 minutes with no code change

risk.note: A CDN setting toggle.

prerequisites: Store is behind Cloudflare or a similar CDN
steps: Check the waterfall for rocket-loader.min.js and rewritten script types in view-source.
If present, go to Cloudflare > Speed > Optimization > Content Optimization and turn off Rocket Loader.
Turn off Scrape Shield and Email Obfuscation if enabled.
Purge the cache and re-test.

test.method: Confirm first-party JS chunks now run as soon as they arrive, not after the load event.

title: On a framework storefront, subset self-hosted fonts to the characters you actually need
hypothesis: If a custom or framework storefront subsets its fonts to the needed character set, including any local currency symbol, then it stops shipping megabytes of unused characters, because a full character set can ship hundreds of unused glyphs per page.

signal.check: A custom or framework storefront (Next.js, Nuxt, custom React) ships a full font file instead of a subset, or is missing a needed local currency symbol.

expected_effect.size: one site shipped 1.9 MB of an unused Korean serif font on every page before the fix

risk.note: Verify every needed character, including local currency symbols, survives the subset.

prerequisites: Developer access to the framework's font configuration
steps: Use the framework's own font loader, such as next/font/google with subsets: ['latin'], or pyftsubset for a WOFF2 subset.
Confirm the subset keeps every needed character, including the local currency symbol.
Never ship a full CJK or other broad character set TTF file unless the store actually needs it.
Re-test page weight after the subset is live.

test.method: Compare font file weight before and after subsetting.

title: On a framework storefront, mark only the LCP image as priority and set sizes on small images
hypothesis: If we set priority on only the single LCP image and sizes on every small image, then the framework's image optimizer stops serving oversized files to small slots, because without sizes it can serve a 640 px image where a small icon slot needed far less.

signal.check: A Next.js or similar framework storefront has no priority attribute set, or is missing sizes on small images, causing oversized delivery.

risk.note: A prop-level change.

steps: Identify the single LCP image per template.
Set the priority prop on that image only.
Set the sizes prop on every small image so the optimizer does not over-serve it.
Confirm delivered image sizes match the rendered slot in the Network panel.

test.method: Check delivered image sizes for small icons and the LCP image after the change.

title: On a framework storefront, server-render the buy box and top collection tiles
hypothesis: If the main image, name, price and add-to-cart render server-side, and only personal state stays client-side, then the shopper sees the buy box immediately instead of waiting for client JavaScript to build it.

signal.check: The main product buy box or top collection tiles wait on client-side JavaScript to render, delaying LCP.

risk.note: Size server capacity before moving more rendering to the server.

prerequisites: Developer capacity for a rendering change
steps: Identify what currently renders client-side on the product and collection pages.
Server-render the main image, name, price and add-to-cart with getStaticProps and revalidate, or getServerSideProps.
Keep only personal state, such as cart contents, client-side.
Size server capacity for the added render load.

test.method: Check the page source (view-source) for the buy box content before JavaScript runs.

title: On a framework storefront, reserve fixed-height containers or skeletons for content that loads late
hypothesis: If late-arriving content on a framework storefront gets a fixed-height container or a skeleton placeholder, then layout shift stops, because content that pops in without reserved space is what causes CLS.

signal.check: A framework storefront shows content jumping into place after initial paint, with no reserved space or skeleton.

risk.note: A CSS and markup change.

steps: Identify components that render after initial paint.
Add a fixed-height container or skeleton placeholder matching the final rendered size.
Verify on each breakpoint that the placeholder does not clip the real content.

test.method: Watch the throttled load and confirm no jump when the late content arrives.

title: On a framework storefront, set a long image cache TTL and a CDN Vary header so AVIF is not pinned wrong
hypothesis: If we set a 30-day minimum cache TTL and a CDN cache key that includes the Accept header, then the edge stops serving the wrong image format to browsers that support AVIF, because without a Vary rule the CDN can pin the first format it saw as PNG for everyone.

signal.check: A framework storefront's image optimizer serves the wrong format (for example PNG instead of AVIF) to browsers that support the better format, because the CDN cache key ignores the Accept header.

risk.note: A CDN configuration change.

prerequisites: CDN admin access (Cloudflare, CloudFront, or similar)
steps: Set images.minimumCacheTTL to about 30 days in the framework's image config.
On Cloudflare, add a Vary for Images rule or a cache bypass for the image optimization path.
On CloudFront, confirm it honours Vary: Accept for the image path.
Verify the correct format is served to both AVIF-capable and non-capable browsers.

test.method: Request the same image with different Accept headers and confirm the correct format returns for each.

title: Write every fix as a plan with a pass threshold, rollback and dependencies, not just a diagnosis
hypothesis: If every listed fix carries the problem and evidence, the expected gain with its arithmetic, effort and owner, the steps, what to measure and the number that counts as done, the risk and rollback, and what it depends on, then a developer or founder can actually run the plan on Monday, because a diagnosis without this structure cannot be executed.

signal.check: A speed audit lists problems found but does not give each one a pass threshold, an owner, or a rollback plan.

expected_effect.size: one blind test found this structure, not the diagnosis, was the difference between a runnable plan and a general audit

risk.note: A reporting format change.

steps: For each fix, write the problem and the evidence for it.
Write the expected gain and its arithmetic, not just a claim.
Assign effort size and an owner (agent, developer or host).
List concrete steps, what to measure before and after, and the number that counts as done.
Note the risk, the rollback, and what the fix depends on.

test.method: Check that every fix in the plan has all these fields before sharing it.

title: Minify and split CSS and JS by page type, and inline critical CSS, only after images and scripts are done
hypothesis: If CSS and JS are minified and split so a product page does not load checkout code and a category page does not load zoom code, then unused code stops being downloaded and parsed, because minification alone can shrink JS up to 80% in some cases.

signal.check: PSI's minify opportunity flags unminified CSS or JS, or a product page loads checkout-only code.

expected_effect.size: JS can shrink up to 80% with minification as a maximum, not a typical figure

risk.note: Do this only after images, scripts and hosting are already fixed.

prerequisites: Images and script triage already done
steps: Confirm images, scripts and layout stability are already fixed first.
Minify CSS and JS files.
Split code by page type so product pages skip checkout code and category pages skip zoom code.
Ask the app's support, or drop the app, for assets you cannot minify or compress yourself.

test.method: Re-check PSI's minify and unused-code opportunities after the change.

title: Delay non-critical CSS (modals, drawers, filter panels) with the media=print trick
hypothesis: If we load below-fold stylesheets like the cart drawer, size-chart modal and filter panel with media='print' onload='this.media=all', then they stop blocking render, because they style nothing visible at first paint.

signal.check: A stylesheet that only styles a modal, drawer or filter panel is currently render-blocking.

risk.note: Never apply this to in-view styles; it causes unstyled content and worse LCP if misapplied.

steps: Identify stylesheets that only style elements not visible at load.
