Rewrite each as a link tag with media='print' onload="this.media='all'".
Confirm the swap happens in the Network panel; a failed onload leaves the sheet print-only.
Never apply this to a stylesheet a shopper sees before scrolling.

test.method: Watch the Network panel to confirm the media swap fires correctly.

title: Make inlined critical CSS complete for every visually different template
hypothesis: If critical CSS is generated per visually different template rather than once for the whole theme, then elements stop showing unstyled for about a second before jumping into place, because a collection with a banner needs different critical CSS than one without.

signal.check: Elements show unstyled for about a second and then jump, on a theme that lazy-loads its main CSS.

risk.note: Requires per-template generation; test each visually distinct template.

steps: Generate critical CSS separately for each visually different template (for example collection with a banner vs without).
Serve it inline from theme.liquid via a snippet.
Add reserve rules for anything still moving after the inline CSS loads.
Recheck the Lighthouse trace for a styled first second with no unstyled flash.

test.method: Watch the Lighthouse trace for the first second on each template.

title: On WordPress and WooCommerce, unload cart, checkout and block styles from every page without a cart
hypothesis: If we unload WooCommerce cart, checkout and block-style files from pages that have no cart, then those pages stop loading files they never use, because these are the files most often left loading everywhere on WooCommerce sites.
does_not_apply_when: Shopify and other platforms without WooCommerce-style global asset loading

signal.check: A GTmetrix waterfall on a WooCommerce landing page with no cart shows cart, checkout or block-style CSS and JS loading anyway.

expected_effect.size: one demo found 13 WooCommerce files loading unnecessarily in one group

risk.note: Write down what was unloaded; re-enable if a page later adds a mini cart.

prerequisites: Asset CleanUp or an equivalent per-page unload plugin
steps: Run a waterfall audit on a page with no cart to see which WooCommerce files still load.
Open the Asset CleanUp metabox for that page and unload files by plugin group.
Keep anything you are unsure about, and write down what you unloaded.
Re-enable specific files if a later feature (such as a mini cart) needs them.

test.method: Re-run the waterfall on the page after unloading and confirm the removed files are gone.

title: Fix render-blocking JavaScript ahead of the main image, and favor server rendering at rebuild
hypothesis: If we cut render-blocking JavaScript that sits ahead of the main image, or choose server-side or hybrid rendering over a fully client-rendered app at rebuild, then the main content shows sooner, because a client-rendered single-page app waits on JavaScript to show anything.

signal.check: The Network waterfall shows scripts loading ahead of the hero or main image, or the page is a client-rendered single-page app with no server-rendered content.

expected_effect.size: unknown, this pattern is called out as the one to avoid 'at all cost'

risk.note: Moving to server-side rendering is a larger rebuild decision; size server capacity first.

steps: Check the waterfall order for scripts loading before the main image or hero.
Where a carousel plugin hides an already-downloaded image until its JS runs, show the image plainly outside the carousel path instead.
At rebuild time, prefer server-side or hybrid rendering over a fully client-rendered app.
Size server capacity before moving rendering to the server.

test.method: Check whether the main image appears as soon as it downloads, without waiting on JS.

title: Remove entrance effects, fade-ins and preloader bars on in-view elements
hypothesis: If we remove fade-in, slide-in and preloader effects on the hero, first slide, main product image and header, then those elements display as soon as they download, because effects need a library to load first and delay display.

signal.check: The hero, first slide, main product image or header has a fade-in, slide-in or preloader effect applied.

risk.note: A CSS or code removal; check the design team is fine losing the effect on these elements.

steps: Identify entrance effects on the hero, first slide, main product image and header.
Remove the effect library or class for these specific elements.
Confirm the plain image displays as soon as it downloads.

test.method: Watch the throttled load and confirm no fade or slide delay on these elements.

title: Trigger pop-ups on exit intent or a time delay, never on page load
hypothesis: If pop-ups fire on exit intent or after a time delay instead of immediately on load, then the initial page load carries less weight and shoppers are not interrupted before they see the page.

signal.check: A pop-up app or script fires immediately when the page loads.

risk.note: A trigger setting change in the pop-up app.

steps: Open the pop-up app's trigger settings.
Switch the trigger from page load to exit intent or a time delay.
Confirm the pop-up no longer fires immediately on a fresh load.

test.method: Load the page fresh and confirm the pop-up does not fire immediately.

title: On a headless storefront, return only the fields a tile or page actually needs from the API
hypothesis: If the storefront API returns only the fields a collection tile or page actually displays, then payload size drops, because sending the full product object for a simple tile wastes bandwidth and parse time.

signal.check: A collection tile's API response includes the full product object instead of only the fields shown on the tile.

risk.note: A backend and front-end coordination task; do not use caching to hide a slow or unstructured API instead of fixing it.

prerequisites: Developer access to the API layer
steps: Inspect the API response for a listing tile.
Identify fields the tile does not display.
Trim the query or endpoint to return only the fields shown.
Coordinate the change between API and front-end developers.

test.method: Compare the API response payload size before and after trimming.

title: Add font-display: swap to every @font-face rule, including every weight and italic
hypothesis: If every @font-face rule carries font-display: swap, then text never hides waiting for a custom font on a slow connection, because without it the price and Buy button text can go invisible until the font arrives.

signal.check: A search of @font-face rules in the theme finds one or more without font-display: swap, especially on price, CTA or headline weights.

risk.note: A CSS property addition.

steps: Search the theme code for @font-face.
Add font-display: swap; just under font-family on every rule missing it.
Cover every weight and italic style used, not just the default.

test.method: Test on a throttled connection and confirm a fallback font shows text immediately, then swaps.

title: Keep about 3 font variations at most, and load only the fonts a page needs
hypothesis: If we cut down to about 3 font weights and styles and only load what a given page uses, then font weight drops, because 5 or 10 weights loaded for a single occurrence is not worth their cost.

signal.check: The theme loads 5 or more font weights or styles, several of which are used in only one or two places.

risk.note: A design review; confirm no needed weight gets cut.

steps: Inventory every custom font weight and style actually used across the site.
Cut down to about 3 variations at most.
Load only the fonts a given page actually uses, not the full set everywhere.

test.method: Count loaded font files before and after the cut.

title: Self-host fonts as WOFF2, or use the platform's built-in fonts, instead of calling Google Fonts
hypothesis: If we self-host fonts as WOFF2 or use the platform's built-in theme fonts, then the page stops making a third-party request to fonts.googleapis.com, removing that connection and DNS lookup from the load.

signal.check: The waterfall shows a request to fonts.googleapis.com or another external font host, with no strong design reason for a custom font.

risk.note: A hosting change; verify the font still renders correctly after self-hosting.

steps: On Shopify, use the theme's built-in fonts unless there is a strong design reason for a custom one.
On WordPress, download WOFF2 files for the needed fonts and upload them as custom fonts in the theme or builder.
Switch the body and heading font variables to the local versions.
Rerun a waterfall check and confirm no request to fonts.googleapis.com remains.

test.method: Check the waterfall for any remaining external font host requests.

title: Style the fallback font to match the custom font's size and line height
hypothesis: If the fallback font is styled to the same size and line height as the custom font, then text does not visibly move when the swap happens, because a mismatched fallback shifts layout and adds to CLS.

signal.check: Text visibly resizes or shifts on a throttled connection when the custom font swaps in.

risk.note: A CSS metric-matching adjustment.

steps: Measure the custom font's rendered size and line height for each text style.
Set the fallback font's size and line height to match as closely as possible.
Test on throttled 3G and confirm text does not visibly move at the swap.

test.method: Watch a throttled reload and confirm no visible text shift at the font swap.

title: Diagnose the exact element causing layout shift before fixing it
hypothesis: If we find the specific element causing layout shift with the PSI filmstrip, Lighthouse trace and a throttled watch, then the fix targets the real cause, because most CLS is either a CSS issue or an app widget without reserved space.

signal.check: PSI reports a CLS above 0.1 and no one has identified the specific shifting element yet.

risk.note: A diagnostic step.

steps: Compare PSI filmstrip frames for a new element that pushes content, and check the desktop tab too.
Open the page and Inspect the element PSI outlines as shifting; search any app-like id in the App Store.
Use Lighthouse's View Original Trace to watch for late-appearing elements.
Throttle and watch the load, stopping mid-way to inspect.
Check common causes in order: missing image dimensions, late app widgets, cookie banners, font swap, late body styles, incomplete critical CSS, contradicting CSS, ads and embeds, entrance animations.

test.method: Confirm the identified element matches what Search Console's field CLS points to.

title: Reserve space for every element that arrives after first paint
hypothesis: If we measure the rendered size of app widgets, ads, embeds and iframes and fix their container's width and height in CSS, then those elements stop pushing content when they arrive late.

signal.check: An app widget, ad, embed or iframe injects after first paint with no reserved container size, causing a visible jump.

risk.note: Verify on every breakpoint; a fixed size can clip a responsive widget.

prerequisites: SPD-091 CLS source identified
steps: Measure the rendered size of the late-arriving element.
Add a CSS rule fixing the container's width and height to that size.
Verify on every breakpoint you care about.
Replace an app-only announcement bar with the theme's own version where possible.

test.method: Watch the throttled load and confirm no jump when the element arrives.

title: Fix contradicting CSS rules and move late inline body styles into the head
hypothesis: If we remove a contradicting CSS rule instead of stacking overrides, and move a late body-tag style into the head, then the page stops re-laying-out after first render, because a late style rewrites base CSS after the browser already painted.

signal.check: Two stylesheets set different sizes for the same element, or an inline style in the body tag changes page width or layout after first render.

risk.note: Confirm the intended design with the owner before removing a conflicting rule.

steps: Inspect computed styles for an element with 2 conflicting size rules.
Remove one rule instead of adding another override.
Move any late body-tag style into the head, and wrap desktop-only rules in a media query.
Prefer the theme's own layout width setting over a custom override.
Confirm the intended design with the owner before finalizing.

test.method: Watch the throttled load and confirm the layout no longer changes after first render.

title: Fix CLS and LCP before installing an app-delay snippet
hypothesis: If CLS and LCP are fixed before adding an app-delay snippet, then the snippet actually delivers its blocking-time gain, because the snippet is 'not as effective' while layout shift or LCP is still large.

signal.check: A store with a large CLS or LCP is about to install an app-delay snippet before fixing those first.

risk.note: A sequencing decision.

steps: Check the current CLS and LCP values.
If either is large, fix it before installing an app-delay snippet.
Only add the delay snippet once CLS and LCP are under control, or measure it as a smaller, secondary gain.

test.method: Compare the delay snippet's measured gain with CLS/LCP fixed vs unfixed.
test.read_point: Before and after adding the snippet

title: Name the LCP element per template before trying to fix it
hypothesis: If we name the specific LCP element for each template using PSI Diagnostics, the Web Vitals extension or the waterfall, then the fix targets the right element instead of guessing.

signal.check: LCP is reported as poor on a template and no one has confirmed which specific element (hero, headline or video) is the LCP element.

risk.note: A diagnostic step.

steps: Open PSI Diagnostics > Largest Contentful Paint element for the template.
Cross-check with the Web Vitals extension log, which also splits time into TTFB, load delay and render delay.
Look for a very wide bar in the Network waterfall as a confirming signal.
Record the named element per template before starting any fix.

test.method: Confirm the same element is named by at least 2 of the 3 methods.

title: Run the standard LCP fix order: un-lazy, de-animate, compress, preload, then cut blocking scripts
hypothesis: If we work the LCP fix in order (remove lazy loading and animation, compress, preload, then cut render-blocking scripts ahead of it), then LCP drops in the order most likely to matter, because each step can undo the gain of a later one if done out of order.

signal.check: The LCP element is an image and is lazy-loaded, animated, uncompressed, unpreloaded, or blocked by scripts ahead of it.

expected_effect.size: one case moved from about 5 seconds and a score in the 30s to 43-50, or 50-60 combined with preload

risk.note: Sequential, testable changes on a duplicate theme.

prerequisites: SPD-095 LCP element named
steps: Remove loading='lazy' and lazysizes classes from the LCP image; set eager.
Remove fade-in, slide-in and preloader effects on it, and keep it out of a delayed carousel path.
Compress it to under 250 KB (or under 200 KB for a hero).
Add a preload with fetchpriority='high'.
Cut render-blocking scripts ahead of it and re-check TBT.
Retest 3 times and average.

test.method: Measure LCP after each step, not just at the end.
test.read_point: After each step, averaged over 3 runs

title: If the LCP image downloads fast but paints late, find the script hiding it, not the image
hypothesis: If a throttled test shows the LCP image file arrived but stayed hidden, then the fix is the script hiding it, not the image itself, because a slideshow plugin's JavaScript can delay display of an already-downloaded image.

signal.check: A throttled load shows the LCP image file finished downloading in the Network panel but the image is not visible on screen for some time after.

risk.note: Removing the carousel dependency for the main image.

steps: Throttle the load of the page with the poor LCP.
Watch whether the main image file finishes downloading before it displays.
If it stays hidden, find the script controlling it, often a slideshow plugin.
Show the main image as a plain image outside the carousel's JavaScript path.

test.method: Re-run the throttled test and confirm the image now shows as soon as it downloads.

title: Check TTFB before blaming the image for a poor LCP
hypothesis: If TTFB is under 800 ms, the LCP fix should focus on the front end; if it is over 800 ms, front-end work should still happen first, then TTFB goes to the host, because a slow server response can itself cause a poor LCP.

signal.check: LCP is poor and TTFB has not been checked as a possible contributor.

risk.note: A diagnostic step.

steps: Read TTFB in PSI for the affected template.
If under 800 ms, work the front end (image, scripts, layout).
If over 800 ms, do the front-end work anyway, then take TTFB to the host (see SPD-111).

test.method: Re-measure TTFB after front-end fixes, before deciding whether to escalate to the host.

title: Confirm a TBT fix with a tap test on Add to Cart, not just the score
hypothesis: If we physically tap Add to Cart and the variant picker on a mid-range phone after a TBT fix, then we confirm the interaction actually feels responsive, because a high TBT means Add to Cart can feel unresponsive after a tap even if the lab score improves.

signal.check: A high TBT was fixed with minify, defer or delay changes, but no one has physically tapped Add to Cart to confirm the feel.

risk.note: A verification step.

prerequisites: SPD-056 or SPD-057 TBT fix already applied
steps: Load the product page on a mid-range phone.
Tap Add to Cart and the variant picker several times.
Confirm the response feels instant, not delayed by half a second or more.
Report the tap-test result alongside the lab TBT number.

test.method: Time the felt delay from tap to visible response.

title: Cut JavaScript on the main thread to fix INP on add-to-cart, variant pickers and filters
hypothesis: If we cut, defer or delay app and tracking scripts and lazy-load non-critical components, then INP on add-to-cart and filters improves, because less JavaScript running on the main thread is the only real fix for interaction delay.

signal.check: Field INP is over 200 ms, or shoppers report Add to Cart doing nothing for about half a second.

risk.note: Combine with the defer/delay ideas above; test the interaction after each change.

prerequisites: SPD-056 and SPD-057 already applied where possible
steps: Cut, defer or delay app and tracking scripts (see SPD-056, SPD-057).
Lazy-load non-critical page components.
At rebuild time, consider moving compatible third parties to a web worker.
Track cart completion (an async request) separately from INP, since INP may not include it.

test.method: Measure field INP after the changes and tap-test the affected controls.
test.read_point: 28 days of field data after the change

title: Treat on-site search autocomplete lag as an everyday INP issue, not just a peak-event risk
hypothesis: If we test predictive site-search latency on a normal day, not only during a peak-event load test, then a laggy autocomplete gets fixed before it costs sales, because this issue usually only gets checked as a peak-event brownout risk.

signal.check: The store has on-site search or autocomplete and its response speed has only ever been checked during peak-load testing, if at all.

risk.note: A testing addition.

steps: Type into the site search box on a normal day, on a mid-range phone.
Time how long suggestions take to appear.
If slow, treat it as a standing INP issue and fix it the same way as any other interaction delay, not only before a sale.

test.method: Time autocomplete response on a regular day, not just before a peak event.

title: Track cart-completion time separately from the INP metric
hypothesis: If we track how long the cart-add request takes to finish as its own timing, then a slow async cart response gets caught, because the INP metric may not include the time an async cart request takes to complete.

signal.check: INP looks fine but shoppers report a delay between tapping Add to Cart and seeing it reflected in the cart.

risk.note: A monitoring addition.

prerequisites: Developer access to add timing instrumentation
steps: Add timing around the cart-add API call, separate from the click-response time INP measures.
Track this as its own number in the speed budget.
Investigate if cart completion is slow even when INP looks fine.

test.method: Compare cart-completion timing against INP to see if they diverge.

title: Verify caching and compression from response headers, not a plugin's settings page
hypothesis: If we read the actual response headers for a cache-hit signal and content-encoding, then we know caching and compression are really on, because a plugin's settings screen can show 'enabled' while the response headers say otherwise.

signal.check: Caching or compression is believed to be on because a plugin setting says so, but the response headers have never been checked directly.

risk.note: A verification step.

steps: Open DevTools Network, tick Preserve log, reload with no throttle.
Click the document request and read response headers for a cache-hit signal and content-encoding.
Do not read cache-control alone as proof; it can say no-cache even when caching is active.
Re-verify in incognito with Disable cache unticked.

test.method: Re-check headers after any caching plugin or host setting change.

title: Never cache cart, checkout, account or any visitor-specific page
hypothesis: If cart, checkout, account and any page with visitor-specific data are excluded from every cache layer, then shoppers never see another visitor's cached cart or stale account data.

signal.check: A caching layer is being turned on or expanded and cart, checkout or account pages have not been explicitly excluded.

risk.note: Caching a visitor-specific page can leak another shopper's data; treat this as a hard exclusion, not a preference.

steps: List cart, checkout, account and any other page with visitor-specific data.
Add explicit exclusion rules for these pages in every cache layer (CDN, plugin, server).
Load each excluded page and confirm the response headers show no caching.

test.method: Load cart, checkout and account pages and check response headers show no cache.
test.read_point: After setting up or changing any cache layer

title: Cache static assets long-term with versioned names, and keep prices and stock fresh
lever: static asset TTL and price freshness
hypothesis: If static assets cache for up to a year with versioned file names, while prices and stock get short TTLs with selective invalidation, then repeat visits load instantly without ever showing a stale price.

signal.check: Static assets have short cache lifetimes without versioned names, or a full cache purge happens on every price change.

risk.note: Test a price change end to end after setting selective invalidation.

steps: Set static assets (images, CSS, JS, fonts) to cache up to 1 year, with versioned file names on update.
Set a short TTL with selective invalidation for pages showing prices or stock, or update them via JavaScript on a cached page.
Test: change a price in admin, reload the product page and a category page listing it, and confirm the price updates while the rest stays cached.

test.method: Change a price and reload the product and a category page listing it.

title: Defer session creation until first add-to-cart or login so anonymous browsing stays cacheable
hypothesis: If a platform waits to create a session cookie until the shopper's first add-to-cart or login, then anonymous browsing pages stay fully cacheable, because a session created on the very first hit forces every page to be treated as dynamic.

signal.check: Response headers on an anonymous first visit already show a session cookie being set before any add-to-cart or login.

risk.note: A platform-level session behavior change; verify cart and login still work correctly.

prerequisites: Platform allows deferring session creation
steps: Check response headers on an anonymous first hit for a session cookie.
If the platform allows it, configure session creation to wait until first add-to-cart or login.
Confirm anonymous pages are now served from cache.

test.method: Check headers on an anonymous visit before and after the change.

title: Turn on full-page caching on self-hosted stores and retest cart and checkout after
hypothesis: If we ask the host by name for Redis, Varnish or an integrated HTTP cache and turn it on, then pre-rendered HTML serves instantly for anonymous visitors, as long as cart and checkout are re-tested and stay excluded.
does_not_apply_when: Shopify, where caching is already managed by the platform

signal.check: A self-hosted store (WooCommerce, Shopware or similar) has no full-page caching layer active.

risk.note: Test cart and checkout end to end after enabling; a misconfigured full-page cache can serve stale or wrong content.

prerequisites: Host or IT admin access
steps: Ask the host by name whether Redis, Varnish or an integrated HTTP cache is available.
Turn it on and confirm pre-rendered HTML serves for anonymous visitors.
Exclude cart, checkout and account pages explicitly.
Test cart, add-to-cart and checkout end to end after enabling.

test.method: Test cart, add-to-cart and checkout, and re-check response headers for cache hits on static pages.

title: Set up a CDN for static assets, picked by traffic geography, targeting an 80%+ hit rate
hypothesis: If we set up a CDN for static assets, sized to the store's traffic geography, and monitor for an 80%+ hit rate, then distant visitors see a real latency cut, because a CDN can cut 200 to 800 ms for visitors far from the origin server.
does_not_apply_when: Shopify, which already serves through Fastly

signal.check: A self-hosted store with customers in several regions has no CDN in front of its static assets, or an existing CDN's hit rate has never been checked.

expected_effect.size: CDN latency cut 200 to 800 ms for distant visitors, per one source citing Cloudflare

risk.note: CDN setup; a low hit rate signals misconfiguration to fix, not a reason to abandon it.

steps: Pick a CDN by traffic geography: a basic single-region CDN, or a global edge network for wide reach.
Start with static assets: images, CSS, JS, fonts.
Set cache keys to include content-changing parameters like page number, and exclude tracking parameters like UTM.
Set automatic invalidation on image updates and deploys.
Monitor hit rate in the CDN dashboard and target 80% or more.

test.method: Check the CDN dashboard's hit rate weekly after setup.

title: Match the hosting tier to monthly order volume
hypothesis: If we move off shared hosting to a VPS or managed cloud once the store passes about 100 orders a month, then hosting stops being the speed bottleneck as traffic grows.

signal.check: A self-hosted store on shared hosting is doing 100 or more orders a month, or growing fast toward that line.

expected_effect.size: heuristic: shared hosting ($1-15/mo) fits a new low-traffic store; VPS or managed cloud ($20-50/mo) at 100+ orders a month

risk.note: A hosting migration; compute ROI against cart abandonment and AOV first.

prerequisites: Monthly orders, AOV, cart abandonment rate
steps: Check current monthly order volume against the 100-order heuristic.
Compute ROI of upgrading using cart abandonment rate and AOV.
If justified, move from shared hosting to a VPS or managed cloud plan.
Add a CDN on top if the store serves international customers.

test.method: Measure TTFB before and after the hosting upgrade.

title: Call the host with the 4 key questions only after front-end fixes are measured
hypothesis: If we contact the host only after images and plugins are fixed and re-measured, with 4 specific questions (PHP version, Redis or Varnish, full-page cache, HTTP/3), then the host has something concrete to answer instead of pointing back at unoptimized content.

signal.check: TTFB is still over 800 ms after front-end fixes are done and measured, and the host has not yet been contacted with specific questions.

risk.note: A conversation, not a technical change; confirm the answers are correct before assuming they are fixed.

prerequisites: Front-end fixes done and re-measured
TTFB measured over 800 ms
steps: Confirm images and plugins are already fixed and re-measured.
Contact the host or in-house admin with 4 questions: PHP version (want 8.2+)? Redis or Varnish active? Full-page cache serving pre-rendered HTML? HTTP/3 on?
Ask them to confirm caching and compression headers are present.
Re-measure TTFB and LCP after any change they make, and test cart and checkout.

test.method: Re-measure TTFB and test cart/checkout after the host's changes.

title: List the dynamic steps at risk of a peak-event slowdown before a big sale
hypothesis: If we list add-to-cart, checkout, login and search as the steps most likely to slow down under peak load, then the team knows what to load-test, because slowdowns in these steps ('brownouts') are more common than a full site crash.

signal.check: A big sale, drop, or limited-inventory launch is planned and no one has listed which dynamic steps are at risk of slowing under load.

risk.note: A planning step.

prerequisites: A peak sale or launch date confirmed, 2 to 4 weeks out
steps: List add-to-cart, checkout, login and site search as the at-risk dynamic steps.
Note which of these run through third-party services (payment, fraud, search) that could also slow down.
Share the list with whoever handles capacity planning for the event.

test.method: Confirm the list covers every dynamic step shoppers touch during checkout.

title: Load-test the at-risk dynamic steps before a peak event and decide what each does under load
hypothesis: If we load-test add-to-cart, checkout, login and search before a peak event, then the team can decide in advance whether each queues, throttles or falls back to a static page, instead of finding out live during the sale.

signal.check: A peak sale is planned and the dynamic steps have never been load-tested under simulated peak traffic.

expected_effect.size: PetSmart's Black Friday pages slowed to 7.7-13.84 seconds without this kind of preparation, per one source

risk.note: Load testing production can itself cause a slowdown; coordinate the timing with the host.

prerequisites: SPD-111 at-risk steps listed
Host or platform capacity check done
steps: Check memory and bandwidth limits and projected peak load with the platform or host.
Load-test each at-risk dynamic step.
Decide in advance what each step does under load: queue, throttle, or a static fallback.
Document the decision for each step.

test.method: Run the load test and confirm each step's behavior matches the planned decision.
test.read_point: Before the event, with enough time to fix any surprise

title: Consider a virtual waiting room for a limited-inventory drop
hypothesis: If a limited-inventory launch uses a virtual waiting room instead of letting the site crash under the surge, then shoppers see an orderly queue instead of an error page, because most surveyed shoppers preferred a queue to an error.
does_not_apply_when: Stores without limited-inventory drops or flash launches

signal.check: A limited-inventory drop or flash launch is planned and the store has no plan for handling a traffic surge beyond normal hosting.

expected_effect.size: 84% of surveyed shoppers preferred a queue to an error page, per one vendor-cited figure

risk.note: This is an infrastructure decision that belongs with 05-SET-store-setup for implementation.

prerequisites: A confirmed limited-inventory launch date
steps: Estimate expected surge traffic for the drop.
Decide whether a virtual waiting room is worth the cost for this specific launch.
If yes, set it up and test it before the launch.
Coordinate the decision with whoever handles infrastructure for the store.

test.method: Test the waiting room with a simulated surge before the real launch.

title: Freeze app installs and theme changes during a peak-event window
hypothesis: If app installs and theme changes are frozen for the event window, then no untested change can slow down or break the site during the highest-stakes traffic of the year.

signal.check: A major sale is approaching and no change freeze has been announced or scheduled.

risk.note: A calendar and communication step.

steps: Set a change-freeze window starting a few days before the event through its end.
Communicate the freeze to the team, agency and any developer working on the store.
Keep a tested rollback path ready in case an emergency fix is unavoidable during the window.

test.method: Confirm no app install or theme change happened during the freeze window.
test.read_point: During and after the event window

title: Clean the WooCommerce database on a schedule
hypothesis: If old revisions, expired transients and orphaned metadata are cleaned on a schedule, then the database stops bloating over time, because these leftovers slow every query that touches the affected tables.
does_not_apply_when: Shopify and other platforms without a self-managed database

signal.check: A WordPress or WooCommerce store has never run a database cleanup tool, or has not run one in months.

risk.note: Back up the database before running a cleanup tool.

prerequisites: Database backup taken first
steps: Back up the database.
Run a cleanup tool (such as WP-Optimize) to remove old revisions, expired transients and orphaned metadata.
Identify and remove or cache any plugin running heavy queries on every page load.
Schedule this cleanup to run regularly, not as a one-off.

test.method: Measure TTFB before and after the cleanup.

title: Replace standard video embeds with lite embeds that load a thumbnail first
hypothesis: If we replace a standard YouTube or similar embed with a lite embed, then the page loads a small thumbnail instead of the full player, because a standard embed costs almost 1 MB and a fixed-size iframe before the shopper even presses play.

signal.check: The Network tab shows player JS loading at page load, before the shopper clicks play, on any video embed.

expected_effect.size: a lite embed loads a thumbnail about 15 KB versus almost 1 MB for a standard embed

risk.note: Replacing the embed component; test that clicking still plays the video correctly.

steps: Check the Network tab before clicking play to see if the player JS already loaded.
Replace the standard embed with a lite-embed component that shows a thumbnail and loads the player only on click.
Test that clicking the thumbnail correctly starts the video.

test.method: Compare page weight before and after the swap, and confirm the video still plays.

title: Turn off video autoplay on mobile and set preload=none
hypothesis: If mobile video autoplay is turned off and preload is set to none, then mobile shoppers are not forced to download video data before choosing to watch, showing a static thumbnail and play button instead.

signal.check: A video on the site autoplays on mobile load, or has no preload='none' attribute set.

risk.note: An attribute change.

steps: Find every video element with autoplay enabled on mobile.
Turn off autoplay and show a static thumbnail with a play button instead.
Set preload='none' on every video tag.

test.method: Load the page on a phone and confirm no video downloads or plays until tapped.

title: Replace every animated GIF with an MP4 video
hypothesis: If we replace animated GIFs with an MP4 in a video tag, then the same motion costs far less bandwidth, because GIF is a much less efficient format for motion than compressed video.

signal.check: A search of the site finds one or more animated GIF files still in use.

risk.note: A format swap.

steps: Search the site for .gif files.
Convert each to a compressed MP4 video.
Replace the GIF with a video tag using preload='none'.

test.method: Compare file weight before and after the swap.

title: Use 301 permanent redirects, never 302, and remove redirect chains
hypothesis: If every permanent move uses a 301 redirect and no page redirects to another redirect, then each visit adds no extra round trip, because a redirect chain forces the browser through multiple hops before the real page loads.

signal.check: The redirect list or a site crawl shows a 302 used for a permanent move, or a URL that redirects to another redirect.

risk.note: A redirect configuration fix.

steps: Export the redirect list, or run a crawl.
Replace any 302 used for a permanent move with a 301.
Find and remove any chain where a URL redirects to another redirect.

test.method: Crawl the site again and confirm no chains and no misused 302s remain.

title: Find and fix broken links to images, CSS and JS
hypothesis: If a broken link checker finds and we fix every 404 to an image, CSS or JS file, then the page stops wasting requests on files that never arrive, and stops missing styles or behavior those files were meant to provide.

signal.check: A broken link checker has never been run, or has not been run recently, on the store.

risk.note: A cleanup task.

steps: Run a broken link checker across the site.
Filter for 404s on images, CSS and JS files specifically.
Fix the link or remove the reference for each one.

test.method: Re-run the broken link checker after the fixes.

title: Build a custom 404 page that points to the top categories
hypothesis: If a broken or old URL lands on a custom 404 page with links to the top 2 categories, then a lost shopper has somewhere useful to go instead of leaving on a dead end.

signal.check: Visiting a broken or removed URL shows the platform's default 404 page instead of a custom one with category links.

risk.note: A page design task.

steps: Visit a known-bad URL and check what the current 404 page shows.
Design a custom 404 page linking to the top 2 revenue categories.
Publish it as the store's 404 page.

test.method: Visit a bad URL and confirm the custom 404 page shows.

title: Remove mobile checkout form steps and offer an express wallet option where the platform allows
hypothesis: If we cut mobile checkout form steps and add an express wallet option like Shop Pay where available, then mobile checkout completion improves, because a delay at checkout loses impulse buyers who already decided to buy.

signal.check: Mobile checkout has several form steps and no express wallet option is enabled or visible.

expected_effect.size: Shop Pay is a vendor-claimed 1.91x mobile checkout-to-order rate; treat as an example, not a promise

risk.note: A checkout configuration change; verify the platform actually supports removing the steps.

prerequisites: Confirm platform checkout customization limits
steps: Count current mobile checkout form steps and fields.
Remove steps the platform allows removing.
Enable an express wallet checkout option if available and not already on.
Test the full flow on a phone after the change.

test.method: Track mobile checkout-to-order rate before and after.

title: Test cart drawer, add-to-cart and checkout after every cache, protocol, script or app change
hypothesis: If we test cart drawer, add-to-cart and checkout after every cache, protocol, script or app change, then a broken buying flow gets caught before shoppers hit it, because these are the steps most likely to break silently from a speed change.

signal.check: A cache, protocol, script or app change was made recently and cart, add-to-cart and checkout have not been re-tested since.

risk.note: A regression test practice.

steps: After any cache, protocol, script or app change, add an item to the cart.
Open the cart drawer and change quantity.
Walk through checkout to the payment step.
Fix immediately if anything is broken or slow, before moving to the next change.

test.method: Run this test after every relevant change, not just at the end of a project.
test.read_point: After every cache, protocol, script or app change

title: Test account, login and order-history page speed for subscription and repeat-purchase stores
hypothesis: If we test account, login and order-history page speed for a subscription or high-repeat-purchase store, then a slow returning-customer experience gets caught, because this playbook does not otherwise cover these pages.
does_not_apply_when: One-off purchase stores with little repeat traffic to account pages

signal.check: The store runs subscriptions or has high repeat purchase, and account, login or order-history pages have never been speed-tested.

risk.note: A test-coverage addition.

steps: Add account, login and order-history pages to the standard speed test list.
Run PageSpeed Insights on each, mobile and desktop.
Fix any that show a poor score using the same methods used elsewhere on the store.

test.method: Track speed on these pages as part of the regular audit cycle.

title: Test the post-purchase upsell and thank-you page for speed
hypothesis: If we test the post-purchase upsell and thank-you page for speed, then a slow page does not lose an add-on sale the shopper already agreed to make, because this page sits right after the hardest conversion step already succeeded.
does_not_apply_when: Stores with no post-purchase upsell offer

signal.check: The store runs post-purchase upsells and the thank-you or upsell page has never been included in a speed audit.

risk.note: A test-coverage addition.

prerequisites: Store runs post-purchase upsells
steps: Add the thank-you and post-purchase upsell page to the standard test list.
Run a speed test on it, mobile and desktop.
Fix any heavy images or scripts found.

test.method: Track upsell take rate alongside page speed.

title: Test any live shipping-cost or delivery-date calculator on cart and checkout for speed
hypothesis: If we test a live shipping-cost or delivery-date calculator for speed on cart and checkout, then a slow calculator does not delay the last step before payment, because shoppers are closest to abandoning right at that moment.
does_not_apply_when: Stores with no live shipping or delivery-date calculator

signal.check: The store shows a live shipping cost or delivery-date estimate on cart or checkout, and its response time has never been checked.

risk.note: A test-coverage addition.

prerequisites: Store has a live shipping or delivery-date calculator
steps: Enter an address or postal code in the calculator on cart and checkout.
Time how long the estimate takes to appear.
If slow, flag the integration for a developer to investigate.

test.method: Time the calculator's response on a mid-range phone.

title: Write a developer brief instead of hand-editing complex theme code without one
hypothesis: If a fix that needs theme logic (responsive widths in a custom section, per-template critical CSS, SSR, API field selection) is written as a brief with the page, element, measured before state and target, then a developer can execute it correctly the first time.

signal.check: A fix needs custom theme logic or code beyond safe settings changes, and no developer brief exists yet.

risk.note: A documentation practice.

steps: Identify fixes that need code the operator cannot safely write themselves.
For each, write the page, the element, the measured before state and the target.
Include the rule and procedure it comes from, an acceptance test and a rollback plan.
Hand the brief to the developer instead of a vague description.

test.method: Confirm the developer's delivered fix matches the acceptance test in the brief.
test.read_point: After the developer delivers the fix

title: Write a host brief with the 4 key questions instead of guessing at server settings
hypothesis: If we send the host a brief with TTFB per template, the headers seen, the 4 questions, and peak-event dates, then the host can act on specific evidence instead of a vague 'the site is slow' report.

signal.check: TTFB is over 800 ms after front-end work and no structured brief has been sent to the host.

risk.note: A documentation practice.

prerequisites: SPD-110 host questions and TTFB measured
steps: Write TTFB per template and the response headers seen so far.
List the 4 questions: PHP version, Redis or Varnish, full-page cache, HTTP/3.
Add any peak-event dates and expected load.
Send as a short email or support ticket.

test.method: Confirm the host's reply answers all 4 questions with specifics.

title: Prove every fix with averaged before/after lab runs plus the field metric moving in 28 days
hypothesis: If every fix is proven with averaged lab runs on the same page, device and tool, plus the field metric moving in the expected direction after 28 days, then a claimed fix is backed by real evidence, not a single lucky run.

signal.check: A fix is being reported as done without a before/after average and without a plan to check field data 28 days out.

risk.note: A reporting discipline.

prerequisites: SPD-001 baseline done
steps: Record page, device, tool, and the 3-run average before and after the change, on the same date each way.
Note any other changes made in the same batch.
Set a 28-day reminder to check the field metric and Search Console.
State clearly in the report what is measured and what is only an example from a source.

test.method: Compare the averaged before/after numbers, then the field metric at 28 days.

title: Exercise every affected app and tracking event after any loading change, before calling it done
hypothesis: If we exercise reviews, upsells, loyalty, forms, chat and pixels fully after any defer, delay, unload, remove or cache change, then a broken feature is caught before it reaches shoppers, since script URLs can also change after an app update.

signal.check: A loading change (defer, delay, unload, remove, cache) was made and the affected apps and tracking events have not been fully exercised since.

risk.note: A verification step.

steps: List every app and tracking event affected by the loading change.
Exercise each one fully: reviews, upsells, loyalty, forms, chat, pixels, consent.
Re-check after any subsequent app update, since script URLs can change.

test.method: Function-test each affected feature and confirm tracking events fire once, correctly.
test.read_point: Immediately after the change, and after any future app update

title: Keep a tested rollback path ready before touching anything, especially during a peak sale window
hypothesis: If a tested rollback path is kept ready before any change, and we revert only the single change that broke something rather than the whole batch, then a mistake costs minutes instead of hours, especially during a peak sale window.

signal.check: A change is about to be made with no confirmed rollback path, or several changes are batched so a single broken one cannot be reverted alone.

risk.note: This is itself the risk-reduction practice.

prerequisites: SPD-014 duplicate theme or staging in use
SPD-030 one-change-at-a-time discipline
steps: Keep the original theme copy or the pre-change setting on hand before any change.
Make one change at a time so a broken feature points to a single cause.
Revert only that single change if something breaks, not the whole batch.
Before touching anything during a peak sale window, confirm the rollback path is tested and ready.

test.method: Practice a rollback on staging before relying on it live.
test.read_point: Before any live change, and before any peak sale window

title: Disable dynamic checkout (wallet) buttons if unused, or delay them to first interaction
hypothesis: If dynamic checkout buttons are disabled when shoppers do not use them, or delayed to first interaction when kept, then their demanding script stops loading at first paint on every product page.

signal.check: Dynamic checkout (wallet) buttons load their script at first paint on product pages, and usage data has never been checked.

expected_effect.size: unknown, trade-off unmeasured in the source

risk.note: Delaying the button means it appears late; test the trade-off before shipping widely.

prerequisites: Dynamic checkout button usage data
steps: Check whether shoppers actually use the dynamic checkout button.
If unused, disable it in theme settings.
If kept, remove its script from content_for_header (see SPD-059) and inject it on first interaction.
Test on a duplicate theme and accept that the button now appears slightly later.

test.method: Measure page weight and score with the button disabled or delayed vs at first paint.

title: Read PageSpeed Insights' 'reduce unused JavaScript' warning correctly before editing any app code
hypothesis: If we treat 'reduce unused JavaScript' as code unused at test time, not code that is useless, then the fix is to remove leftovers and defer, delay or load conditionally, instead of making risky line-by-line edits to app code the store does not own.

signal.check: A PSI report flags 'reduce unused JavaScript' and someone is about to hand-edit third-party app code in response.

risk.note: Editing app code you do not own can break on the next app update; avoid it.

steps: Read the 'reduce unused JavaScript' flag as unused on this specific page, not globally useless code.
Check first whether the flagged script is leftover residual code (SPD-054).
If it is a real app script, defer, delay or load it conditionally by template (SPD-056, SPD-063) instead of editing it.
Do not make line-by-line edits to app code you do not own.

test.method: Re-check the flag after removing leftovers and adjusting loading, without editing app code directly.

title: Follow a fixed image-prep order to avoid redoing earlier steps
hypothesis: If we always resize, crop, convert format, compress, then name and add alt text, in that order, before uploading a batch of images, then we avoid redoing earlier steps, because doing them out of order, such as compressing before resizing, creates rework.

signal.check: A team preps product or content images in an ad-hoc order and keeps redoing earlier steps, or resizes an image again after it was already compressed and named.

risk.note: A process change only; nothing on the live site changes.

steps: Resize each image to its target dimensions first.
Crop one image at a time to match its final aspect ratio; never crop in bulk.
Convert to the final format: JPEG for photos, PNG only for transparency.
Compress once, from the resized and converted file, not from the original a second time.
Rename the file and write alt text last, right before upload.
Upload once to the media library and reuse the same file everywhere it is needed.

test.method: Compare a batch prepped in this fixed order against a prior ad-hoc batch for repeated steps and total prep time.
test.read_point: After the first batch run in this order

title: Decide per image whether to resize, compress, or both before fixing it
hypothesis: If we check each flagged image's dimensions against its display box and its file size against our ceiling before touching it, then we resize only oversized images and compress only heavy ones, because treating every flagged image the same way wastes time on ones that do not need that fix.

signal.check: A speed report flags several images and the team is about to resize or compress all of them the same way without checking which fix each one actually needs.

risk.note: A diagnosis step before any change.

steps: Inspect each flagged image's intrinsic size versus its rendered display box.
Check its file size against the store's ceiling.
Oversized in dimensions: resize first, then check if it still needs compression.
Right-sized but heavy: compress only.
Small and already under the ceiling: leave it alone.
Record the decision so the next audit does not repeat the check on the same image.

test.method: Compare total time spent and bytes saved against fixing every flagged image the same way regardless of cause.
test.read_point: After clearing one batch of flagged images

title: Use a lazysizes-style JS library for finer control than native lazy loading
hypothesis: If we swap native loading=lazy for a small JS library such as lazysizes on below-fold images, then we get a placeholder and finer control over the load trigger, because native lazy loading has no placeholder and little trigger tuning.
does_not_apply_when: Any in-view image, which must never be lazy loaded by any method

signal.check: Below-fold images use native loading=lazy and the team wants a placeholder or finer control over when images swap in, or native lazy loading is not behaving consistently across older devices.

expected_effect.size: one presenter's opinion: slightly better than native lazy loading

risk.note: Adds a JS dependency; verify it does not itself delay the images it should speed up.

prerequisites: Below-fold images identified
steps: Add the lazysizes script, or an equivalent small library, to the theme.
Set each below-fold image's src to a placeholder pixel and its real URL in data-src.
Add the library's lazy-load class to each of those images.
Never apply this to the hero, logo, first slide or any other in-view image.
Verify in the Network panel that in-view images still download at once and others only on scroll.

test.method: Compare page weight and perceived load on a throttled connection with native lazy loading versus the library.
test.read_point: After swapping a template's below-fold images

title: Ask an app's support team to fix an uncompressed asset, or drop the app
hypothesis: If we contact an app's support team about an asset we cannot minify or compress ourselves, such as a file served from the app's own server, then the app either fixes it or we get a clear reason to drop it, because some blocking assets live outside our own code and are not ours to edit directly.

signal.check: A speed report flags an app's script or asset as unminified or uncompressed, and the file is served from the app's own domain, not the store's theme.

risk.note: An outreach step; no change to the store until the app responds.

prerequisites: App identified as the owner of the flagged asset
steps: Confirm the flagged asset is served by an app, not the store's own theme.
Contact the app's support team with the specific finding: file, size, and the flag it triggered.
If they fix it, re-test to confirm the gain.
If they cannot or will not, weigh the app's value against its speed cost and consider dropping it.

test.method: Re-run the speed report after the app's fix, or after removing the app.
test.read_point: After the app responds, or after removal

title: Turn off default platform bloat features that ship on by default
hypothesis: If we disable default platform features nobody uses, such as an emoji-detection script, dashicons for logged-out visitors, pingbacks and unused block-editor CSS, then logged-out pages carry less dead weight, because these ship turned on by default whether or not the store uses them.

signal.check: A waterfall or asset audit on WordPress or a similar platform shows requests for an emoji script, dashicons, pingback endpoints or block-editor CSS on pages that do not use those features.

risk.note: Only disable features confirmed unused, and re-test after.

steps: Open the platform or builder's performance settings.
Tick off each feature the store does not use: emoji script, dashicons for logged-out visitors, pingbacks, unused block-editor CSS.
Skip any toggle tied to a feature the store actually uses.
Save and re-check the waterfall for the removed requests.

test.method: Compare waterfall requests before and after disabling each toggle.

title: Reference theme CSS and JS through a cache-busting asset filter, not a typed URL
lever: CDN cache invalidation for theme assets
hypothesis: If we reference theme CSS and JS through the platform's versioned asset filter instead of typing a static CDN URL, then an edit actually reaches shoppers, because a hardcoded URL carries no version marker and the CDN keeps serving the old cached file.
does_not_apply_when: Platforms without an equivalent versioned asset filter

signal.check: A CSS or JS edit does not show on the live site after a normal cache wait, and the file is referenced by a typed-out URL inside a stylesheet instead of the platform's asset filter.

risk.note: A reference-only change; no visual change if done correctly.

prerequisites: Developer access to theme code
steps: Search theme CSS and JS for hardcoded asset URLs instead of the platform's versioned asset filter.
Replace each one with the versioned filter, such as Shopify's asset_url.
Confirm the rendered URL now carries a version parameter that changes on edit.
Make an edit to the file and confirm it shows live without a manual cache purge.

test.method: Edit the asset and reload the live page to confirm the new version shows immediately.
test.read_point: Right after the next asset edit

title: Find and merge template loops that crawl the same product data twice
hypothesis: If we find template loops that crawl the same collection or product list more than once to check different conditions, and merge them into one pass, then the server does less repeated work per page render, because running the same loop twice over the same data wastes render time for no extra output.

signal.check: A code review of theme templates finds two or more loops crawling the same collection or product list, often left behind when several developers worked on the theme.

risk.note: Confirm the merged loop still outputs every condition the separate loops checked.

prerequisites: Developer access to theme templates
steps: Review theme templates for loops that crawl the same collection or product list more than once.
Confirm each loop's purpose and condition, such as price or tag.
Merge them into a single loop that checks all conditions in one pass.
Use a simpler built-in loop helper where one exists instead of a manual crawl.
Re-test the page and confirm every original condition still works.

test.method: Compare TTFB and server response time on the affected template before and after the merge.

title: Remove or defer Quick View so it stops pre-loading every thumbnail's data
hypothesis: If we remove Quick View from collection pages, or load its product data only on click instead of pre-loading it for every thumbnail, then collection pages stop fetching full product data most shoppers never open, because Quick View by default pre-loads data for every tile on the grid.

signal.check: A collection page's network requests show full product data loading for every thumbnail before any Quick View button is clicked.

expected_effect.size: pre-loads data for 20 to 30 thumbnails per collection page in the source's example

risk.note: Check click-map data first, since some shoppers do use Quick View.

prerequisites: Click-map or analytics data on Quick View usage
steps: Check a click map or analytics for how often shoppers actually use Quick View.
If rarely used, remove it and rely on the full product page.
If it must stay, switch it to load product data only on click, or store a small data set as data attributes and build the popup with JavaScript.
Confirm the popup still works after the change.
Re-test the collection page's network weight.

test.method: Compare network requests and page weight on a collection page before and after.

title: Automate speed testing in the deploy pipeline or on a schedule
hypothesis: If we run PageSpeed Insights or Lighthouse automatically on every deploy or on a schedule, then a regression gets caught before the next manual audit, because a manual monthly check can miss a slowdown introduced between checks.

signal.check: Speed testing happens only when someone remembers to run it by hand, with no automated check tied to deploys or a schedule.

risk.note: A monitoring addition; does not change the live site.

prerequisites: A deploy pipeline or a place to run a scheduled job
steps: Pick a free automation option: the PageSpeed Insights API on a schedule, a GTmetrix monitoring account, or Lighthouse CI in the deploy pipeline.
Set it to test the store's key templates: home, top product, category, cart and checkout.
Set an alert or a failing threshold tied to the store's performance budget.
Review any automated alert the same way as a manual finding.

test.method: Compare how quickly a deliberately introduced regression is caught with automation on versus the prior manual-only cadence.
test.read_point: After the first automated run catches or misses a real change

title: Design the above-the-fold section so the largest element is text, not an image
hypothesis: If the largest visible element above the fold is a text block instead of an image or video, then LCP is faster by design, because text paints as soon as its font is ready while an image or video must first download.

signal.check: A template's LCP element is consistently a hero image or video, and a text-led layout could carry the same message.

risk.note: A design change; confirm it does not weaken the page's persuasive job before shipping it.

steps: Check PageSpeed's named LCP element for each key template.
Where the LCP element is an image or video and a text-led design could carry the same message, mock up a text-first version of that section.
Confirm the text-first version still meets the page's conversion job before shipping it.
Re-test LCP after the change ships.

test.method: Compare LCP before and after switching the section's largest element to text.

title: Share the PageSpeed report's own link instead of relaying findings by hand
hypothesis: If we send PageSpeed Insights' own share link instead of describing the findings in writing, then the developer sees the exact same report, because the link opens the frozen result instead of a fresh re-run that could read differently.

signal.check: A speed finding is being relayed to a developer or agency by a written description or screenshot instead of the tool's own share link.

risk.note: A communication habit; no site change.

steps: Run the PageSpeed Insights test on the page in question.
Use the report's copy-link control to get its share link.
Send that link to the developer or agency instead of a written summary alone.
Ask them to confirm they see the same score and flagged items before starting work.

test.method: Confirm the developer's report matches the shared link's findings before work begins.

title: Run a speed check on any new feature or app before it ships, not only at the next audit
hypothesis: If every new feature, animation or app gets a before-and-after speed test before it goes live, then a slowdown is caught at the moment it is added, because most site changes add weight and a periodic audit can miss the change for weeks.

signal.check: A new feature, animation or app is about to ship, or just shipped, with no speed test run specifically for that change.

risk.note: A gating step, not a change to the site itself.

prerequisites: SPD-001 baseline exists
steps: Before approving a new feature, animation or app for launch, run a speed test on the page it touches.
Ship the change.
Run the same speed test again right after launch.
If it fails the store's performance budget, fix it or hold the launch instead of waiting for the next scheduled audit.

test.method: Compare the before and after speed test for the specific page the change touches.
test.read_point: Immediately before and after the change ships

title: Set fetchpriority=low on non-critical images so they stop competing with the LCP image
hypothesis: If we mark non-critical, far-down-the-page images with fetchpriority=low, then the browser fetches the LCP image first instead of splitting bandwidth with images the shopper has not scrolled to, because a priority hint tells the browser which requests matter less.

signal.check: The LCP image is competing for bandwidth with several other images loading at the same time, and none of them carry a fetchpriority hint.

risk.note: Only mark true outliers low; do not mark everything high or low.

steps: Identify the LCP image and confirm it already has fetchpriority=high or a preload tag.
Identify images far down the page that are not the LCP element.
Add fetchpriority=low to those images.
Re-test LCP to confirm the browser now loads the LCP image first.

test.method: Compare LCP timing before and after setting fetchpriority=low on the non-critical images.

title: On a framework storefront, code-split and lazy-load non-critical UI components
hypothesis: If non-critical first-party UI components, such as a filter panel, a size guide or a secondary carousel, are code-split and lazy-loaded, then their JavaScript downloads only when needed, because a framework's dynamic import lets the browser skip code for parts of the page the shopper has not reached yet.

signal.check: A framework storefront's main JavaScript bundle includes code for components not visible or not needed on first load, such as filters, modals or secondary carousels.

risk.note: Verify the lazy-loaded component still renders correctly and quickly enough when it is needed.

prerequisites: Developer access to the framework's bundler configuration
steps: List first-party UI components not needed for the first paint: filters, modals, secondary carousels, size guides.
Split each into its own bundle using the framework's dynamic import or lazy-loading feature.
Load each bundle only when its component becomes visible or is interacted with.
Test that each component still renders correctly and quickly when triggered.
Re-test the main bundle's weight after the split.

test.method: Compare the initial JavaScript bundle size and page weight before and after code-splitting.

title: Audit plugins for expensive, uncached database queries on every page load
hypothesis: If we check each plugin for database queries it runs on every page load without caching, then we catch a backend slowdown that front-end fixes cannot touch, because a plugin's own uncached query can dominate server response time regardless of how light the page's images and scripts are.

signal.check: TTFB is high, or a page feels slow even after images and scripts are optimized, and no one has checked which plugins run queries on every page load.

risk.note: Confirm the plugin still works correctly after adding caching around its query or removing it.

prerequisites: Developer or hosting access to profile database queries
steps: Ask the developer or host to profile database queries on a slow page.
Identify which plugin or extension triggers each expensive, uncached query.
For a plugin still needed, add caching around its query, or ask the vendor to.
For a plugin not clearly needed, remove it and re-test.
Re-check TTFB after each change.

test.method: Compare TTFB before and after addressing each flagged plugin.
